Satellites are crucial for creating grand tack scenarios that prevent binary stars from becoming too close, and thus influencing planetary formation.  However, the masses of most satellites are unknown as they aren't typically detected through standard astrophysical observations.  We developed numerical codes to simulate the hydrodynamic interactions between a satellite and a star, and found that many satellites actually have masses greater than previously estimated.  By calculating their mass ranges and considering different orbital patterns, we determined that most satellites with periods less than 50 days have masses greater than 1 Earth mass, with many exceeding 10 Earth masses.  These estimates are vital for understanding how satellites affect planetary migration and influence the formation of terrestrial planets in protoplanetary disk systems.  Further research into their detection methods is necessary to observe these satellites directly.  We propose that bodies with masses greater than 10 Earth masses and orbital periods longer than 50 days shouldn't be considered satellites, but rather exomoons.  This distinction is crucial for accurately modeling their influences on planetary migration and the migration of binary stars.  Further studies into their detection and analysis are necessary to better understand these bodies and their effects on celestial systems.  Exomoons with short periods may not influence migration, but those with longer periods at higher masses may impede it, similar to the effects of terrestrial planets.  Consequently, they may shift the binary star configuration and influence the formation of the inner planets.  As such, exomoons hold significant value in shaping our understanding of celestial systems and may contribute substantially to our knowledge of astronomy.  We propose a new category of bodies called "subsatellites" that have masses less than 1 Earth mass and may influence migration differently than both satellites and planets.  This term is crucial for defining their distinct influences on the migration of binary stars and the formation of terrestrial planets.  As such, subsatellites could be considered individual objects rather than a part of a larger system, and may have distinct effects on celestial migration and astronomy.  Further research into their detection and analysis is necessary to validate this category and understand its implications for astronomy. The surge in wireless communication accelerates the risk of hardware components being compromised through radio frequency attacks. To address this, we propose HyperDegrade, a novel approach that optimizes CPU frequencies across multiple cores in a way that enhances resistance to these attacks. We demonstrated that with just a 20% reduction in overall performance, we can develop a 10-factor stronger defense against DEP attacks and a 4.5-factor stronger defense against PLL injection attacks. To support this, we created a scheduling algorithm that can deal with a wide range of power distribution unit configurations and detailed technical documentation for a power management controller used in certain Intel and AMD systems. We also developed a tool called HyperDegrade, capable of efficiently determining the optimal frequency scheduling and a proof-of-concept implementation for x86-64 systems. With HyperDegrade, we were able to develop a 96-core AMD EPYC server prototype that can provide a 12.5-factor stronger defense against DEP attacks and a 5.5-factor stronger defense against PLL injection attacks. This research was presented at the 2023 ASPLOS conference held in Austin, Texas. We have made HyperDegrade available open-source. The code can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/ghasempour/hyperdegrade. The tool and documentation also support research into various power management scenarios and frequency scheduling. The results we obtained with HyperDegrade are listed in the Appendix section. The code has a permissive BSD license. This paper delves into the world of Federated Learning (FL), focusing on its
more advanced form, Pragmatic FL. Within this framework, participants follow
established protocols after considering each other's preferences and goals.
Despite the numerous benefits of Pragmatic FL, it suffers from a significant
weakness it cannot protect user privacy effectively. In fact, we've discovered
a new private invasion tactic called "Privacy Assault," which targets the
flaw in Pragmatic FL and manipulates users' behavior in a way that compromises
their security. We demonstrate this concept through "Lying," a basic Privacy
Assault strategy, and show how it can be executed both centrally and in a
horizontal FL setting. However, we also acknowledge that executing this
assault in a vertical FL scenario appears more complicated. In order to address
this challenge, we developed an algorithm called "Assault-by-Exploitation"
(AEE), capable of carrying out Privacy Assault in a vertical FL scenario for a
single round. AEE employs a combination of reinforcement learning and
exploitation-intense techniques that enables the server to rapidly learn the
users' preferences and exploit this new knowledge to execute a successful
Privacy Assault. We tested both Lying and AEE on various groups of users and
discovered that executing a successful Privacy Assault is generally more
challenging in a vertical FL setting than in a horizontal FL setting but AEE
is highly effective in carrying out Privacy Assault in a single round. In the
process, we also identified a key difference between the two FL settings and
pointed out a potential security risk in the vertical FL scenario but not in
the horizontal FL scenario. In conclusion, we believe this research on Privacy
Assault in a vertical FL setting opens the door to further exploration and
analysis of this type of private invasion tactic. We suggest possible future
research on this topic, including but not limited to, investigating the
difficulty of executing a successful Privacy Assault in a vertical FL setting,
the effects of Privacy Assault on user drop-out rates and model accuracy, and
the potential advantages of adopting a multi-round AEE framework. We also
emphasize that in order to tackle various Privacy Assault strategies that target
the user side, we need to develop more effective and general methods of
mitigating these attacks, such as creating robust FL algorithms that are less
vulnerable to Privacy Assault. We believe this goal is comparable to similar

This paper investigates conformal changes in a compact hypersurface within an (n+1)-dimensional sphere up to a specific Mobius transformation. We establish certain rigidity results for conformally equivalent hypersurfaces with constant scalar curvature under specific mobility assumptions. These results hold true in higher dimensional spaces and provide a means of identifying solutions to a particular conformally invariant equation. This paper provides a follow-up to our previous work where we utilized three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations incorporating full particle interactions to model substructures in developing VSI patterns, and then used these results to create a comprehensive set of images for a range of optical depths and orientations. We have now converted the generated images into synthetic fluxes that mimic observations from the SPITZER and ALMA, and our previous research on global VSI patterns is now reinforced by these simulations. We have also identified key features that consistently emerge and can be broadly categorized into three types: those influenced by the vertical shear, those affected by the initial perturbation, and those related to the VSI patterns themselves. These features include ridges of increased emission just above the inner disk, bands of enhanced emission within the disk, and patterns of decreased emission along the midplane. We have created empirical models of these features, and our simulations demonstrate that even without the influence of VSI patterns, the T Tauri star disks that exhibit similar properties to those in our simulations can already possess these substructures, even when the amplitude of the surface height distribution function is quite small. This, in turn, implies that a specific set of substructures may be distinguishable in a particular range of T Tauri star disks that are subject to VSI and have a specific set of characteristics. These empirical predictions for the dust continuum are derived from the simulations and can be verified with ongoing and future observations from the ALMA and other similar telescopes. This research highlights the significance of considering the shearing inner disk and its impact on the development of VSI patterns and the resulting substructures, as well as the importance of accurately interpreting observed features in T Tauri star disks that are subject to VSI and vertical shear. This may lead to a reevaluation of some previously misinterpreted disk substructures and features, and it provides a foundation for a new area of research that aims to comprehensively explore the effects of VSI and vertical shear on the development of substructures, features, and patterns in protoplanetary disks. This paper introduces the "Big Apple parameter", a new quantity that determines the neutron-star maximum mass, as it represents the point at which neutron stars and stars with neutron skin collapse under strong gravity. By analyzing recent astronomic observations and laboratory experiments involving neutrons and nuclei, we established the "Big Apple" value of 2.765 ± 0.005 solar masses. Notably, this finding aligns with a previous estimate from 2019. By using the "Big Apple" parameter in a model that combines relativistic mean-field theory and quark-phase transitions, we found it helps in identifying specific conditions for neutron stars, including their radius, mass, and density distributions. Additionally, it enables the derivation of a critical parameter for finite nuclei, namely the upper limit for the ratio of their neutron to proton density. This density threshold is essential in explaining various phenomena in the cosmos, such as supernovae explosions and the formation of heavy elements. Finally, we propose the term "Big Apple strength" as a colloquial expression for this parameter, which can be determined from the properties of isolated neutron stars that exhibit pulsar characteristics. These stars, with their inherent magnetic fields, can be found in the Milky Way and other spiral galaxies. Sincerely, W. Weise. Neural language generation models have been the subject of numerous recent studies, with a particular focus on sequence-to-sequence models based on transformer architecture. While these innovations have yielded notable improvements in several areas, including machine translation and text summarization. In contrast, $N$-gram models, which were widely used in the past, have largely been set aside. This work reinvestigates $N$-gram models with a unique twist, incorporating them into neural learning through a residual framework. We demonstrate how a simple $N$-gram model can be employed to generate an extensive corpus of text, which can then be used to train a neural language model through rejection sampling. When used for text augmentation, this approach matches the performance of neural generation, while for topics like conversation flows, it surpasses the capabilities of neural models. This research highlights the versatility and the previously underappreciated potential of $N$-gram models when combined with neural learning. We release our code and generated datasets at https://github.com/ghrua/neural-text-generation-with-ngram.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in real-time has a wide range of practical applications including virtual gaming, animation, and surveillance. Over the past few years, neural networks have significantly improved face reconstruction technology but still struggle with several challenges such as varying lighting conditions, expression changes, and different camera angles. To tackle these difficulties, our innovative solution, SADRNet, introduces a self-alignment dual prediction face reconstruction network that simultaneously generates three distinct outputs for a single input face: a reconstructed face, a face mask, and a direction vector. These components work together to ensure the network is robust against expression and angle information and our results show that SADRNet outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods in multiple challenging scenarios including InertiaFlow, a large expression-based dataset and the widely-used 3D Face in Action Dataset. Code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghr1202/SADRNet.

A labeled ordered tree of height h has h levels of descent, starting from a root node at level 0, and contains n leaves of 1-degree, connected to internal nodes of 2-degree. The set of deepest vertices in the tree includes those with a maximal amount of leaf connectivity at the lowest level. We aim to calculate the distribution and properties of these deepest vertices, as well as identify patterns when the degree of internal nodes is restricted. A "generalized Catalan" formula enables us to determine the number of labeled ordered trees with a specific number of 2-degree internal nodes. By applying this formula, we examine the distribution of the deepest 1-degree vertices, the distribution of the number of the deepest 1-degree vertices, and the distribution of the deepest 2-degree vertices. For the distribution of the number of the deepest 1-degree vertices, we use a transformation to obtain an explicit formula, supported by numerical evidence showing its consistency over various conditions. For the distribution of the deepest 2-degree vertices, we determine an explicit conditional distribution. Both of these distributions hold for rooted binary trees, which are a specific type of labeled ordered trees. We also discuss the relationship between the distribution of the deepest 2-degree vertices and the distribution of the size of the largest subtree in a labeled ordered tree. This property does not extend to binary trees. We conclude by examining the distribution of the deepest 1-degree vertices in a specific class of labeled ordered trees, namely the binary trees, and determine its relationship to the distribution of the size of the largest subtree. This property does not extend to general labeled ordered trees. We derive the distribution of the size of the largest subtree in a binary tree, which can be any nonnegative integer, and confirm that it is equivalent to the distribution of the deepest 1-degree vertex, also any nonnegative integer. This property does not extend to the general labeled ordered trees. We discuss our results and possible approaches to obtaining further insights. We believe our work can be applied to random processes involving the assembly of units at multiple levels of complexity, and to mathematical models such as certain versions of the preferential attachment model. We propose a new model based on the binary tree random process, which enables us to determine the distribution of the deepest 1-degree vertices as any nonnegative integer, and to confirm that it is equivalent to the distribution of the size of the largest subtree in a binary tree, also any nonnegative integer. This paper introduces Informed Optical Character Recognition (iOCR) which is a novel approach that combines artificial intelligence and human judgment to accurately count large sets of handwritten data, significantly reducing errors and inconsistencies.  This innovation was put into practice during the 2020 US presidential election, where iOCR was used to accurately count ballot totals in several crucial states, thus preventing the spread of false information that could have led to public unrest.  Our results show that iOCR's advanced security features and ability to adapt to different handwriting styles and spelling mistakes enable it to correctly count ballot totals with a precision of 99.95%.  Our work offers valuable insights and techniques for addressing the ongoing challenges surrounding the reliable counting of handwritten ballot data.  Our iOCR technology is currently in use by several high-profile election organizations and it has the potential to be applied to similar problems in other fields that involve counting large sets of handwritten data, such as in medical research and historical document analysis.  Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/TrueData/iocr. Decentralized energy systems are gaining popularity, and managing them requires intelligent planning for local assets. This research focuses on a decentralized system consisting of renewable energy sources, consumer units, and storage units, which are connected through a local microgrid. A new self-planning approach for storage is developed to maximize profits in a centralized optimization model, then utilizes trustworthy information to guide its decision-making in a decentralized setting through self-learning artificial neural networks. A real-world scenario based on a community of 12 households in Germany was tested and showed the potential of the developed approach to balance central and decentralized decision-making. A notable finding is that an overreliance on central optimization or machine learning components can lead to exploitable security risks due to their lack of transparency. This issue highlights the significance of transparent storage self-planning in response. This research was presented at the 2020 IEEE Technical Workshop on Advances in High-Performance Smart Grid Applications, which took place in Germany. Some of these forms mimic the gamma function's original integral definitions, despite not originating from them. As an application, it obtains an integral representation of Euler's number $e$. In the process, it also outlines a method for converting certain integral expressions to their hypergeometric form equivalents. One of the derived expressions in fact corresponds to an integral in Gradshteyn and Ryzhik's table of integrals, though it was missing the hypergeometric function component. It is proposed to test for the distinction between light (up, down, strange) and heavy (charm, bottom) quark generations through collision geometries and final-state hadron measurements in p+A and A+A collisions. The soul of this approach lies in the assumption that the distribution of partons participating in the collision is influenced by their mass, constraining the range of soft gluons that surround heavy quarks and influence the formation of hadrons through medium effects. As a result, the generation of heavy and light quarks may differ in their dependence on transverse momentum, initial partonic geometry, and final-state hadron properties. To this end, a new method is introduced that utilizes neural networks to differentiate quarks of a given generation based on p+A and A+A collision data, and a discussion is given of the factors that influence this differentiation, such as the mass of the quarks, their collision energy, and the properties of the hadrons they form. As an illustration, top-quark generation is examined in p+Au and Au+Au collisions at 200 GeV, and the resulting distributions from a neural network are analyzed and compared to theoretical predictions that incorporate the effects of collision geometry and partonic re-scattering. We investigate the drag experienced by a long cylindrical object being pushed through a mixture of granular material and water, where the flow of water is free. We found that the direction of the drag force isn't necessarily aligned with the direction the cylinder is moving, a phenomenon known as anisotropy of resistance. This anisotropy becomes more noticeable as the cylinder's aspect ratio increases. We explain the source of this anisotropy as resulting from the interaction between the water and the granular material at the leading edge of the cylinder, where the water experiences the most resistance and flows most horizontally. This causes the most resistant grains to be located on the sides of the cylinder rather than at its front. As a result, when the cylinder is moved sideways, these side grains move more easily than when it's moved forward, contributing to the anisotropy of resistance. We confirmed our analysis through additional simulations where we fixed the cylinder at an angle and let the mixture settle around it, only to move the cylinder once the mixture had settled. This allowed us to compare the drag force with that of a similar but vertically oriented cylinder. We found that the ratio of the drag forces in these two situations is directly related to the aspect ratio of the cylinder and can be calculated using its dimensions. This calculation considers not just the immediate area around the cylinder but also the effects of the water and grains on each other over a wider distance, which we determined by analyzing the settled grains in the simulation. This research provides a new perspective on drag resistance within complex, three-dimensional environments and highlights the significance of two-phase interactions on the behavior of cylindrical objects. It also offers practical insights for the design of cylinders in various real-world applications, such as pipes in the ground, tree trunks, and ship hulls. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. To better understand this phenomenon, we analyzed triangular flow fluctuations and correlations with elliptical flow. My approach deviates from standard methods as it interprets $v_3$ and $v_2$ as individual and cross-species anisotropic responses to the same initial geometry. This perspective enables the extraction of key information on the system size, shape, and fluctuation characteristics. Notably, I demonstrated that the same collision system produces similar triangular and elliptical flow responses when measured in different centrality ranges. Notably, the anisotropic responses to the same initial geometry also allow for extraction of the number of participating nucleons, transverse overlap area, and initial eccentric and algebraic eccentricity fluctuations. These findings suggest that triangular flow, similar to elliptical flow, lacks specific scaling with collision centrality and instead depends solely on the initial geometry and resulting particle distribution. To further validate these results, we performed similar analyses with the AMPT model, yielding essentially identical outcomes when using default and minimum bias initial state configurations. These findings have significant implications for heavy-ion collisions as they indicate that triangular flow and its fluctuations are primarily determined by the same initial geometry that drives elliptical flow, and as such, may be less sensitive to flow pattern velocity fluctuations. This perspective on triangular flow also provides a more accurate interpretation of Cu+Cu data presented in [6, 7], which showed nearly identical $v_3/\epsilon_3$ responses to Au+Au collisions. To facilitate experimental verification, we performed predictions for $v_3$ and $v_2$ in 54.4, 62.4, 200 GeV Au+Au collisions using a two-particle cumulant method. These results agree with previous measurements and facilitate searches for projected phenomena such as triangular flow's dependence on event orientation and beam energy scaling of anisotropic flow. To this end, we propose a new Cu+Cu data analysis which would involve measuring $v_3$ in different event orientation bins and comparing results with our predictions, along with similar measurements for $v_2$ and $v_3$ in Au+Au collisions. This self-guided approach leverages a motion-aware latent space within a latent representation, which we've termed the "motion cosmos." By doing so, it obtains relevant point features and motion information autonomously. The corresponding code has been made publicly accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyangyin/SMCF-Net. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can independently determine system call permissions by comparing expected system calls to those that actually occur. It then adapts these permissions for the benefit of future operations. In addition to this, it includes a feature called "watchdogs" which allows the user to design custom system call monitoring and response functions using a simple API. We put forward a concrete example of an application using Timeloops, called "watchdog loops", which allows for efficient and secure operation within a narrow system call permission set. We also present a containerized implementation of the famous Apache Kafka application using system call policy watchdog loops. Our results show that Timeloops leads to a significant reduction in system call permissions required, resulting in improved security and performance. Furthermore, it provides a simple and lightweight way for developers to define system call policies without needing extensive knowledge of system call analysis. This in turn enables secure and efficient operation of complex containerized applications. This is particularly evident in our Kafka implementation, which successfully operates within a 64 system call permission set, a significant reduction from the original 350 system call set required for initial deployment. This technology is particularly suitable for use cases such as edge computing and embedded systems. We show that Timeloops can be effectively used to analyze and validate various security hardening guidelines and best practices for system call policies. This is a valuable feature for developers, system administrators and security auditors. This technology has been made open to the public through an open source license. It is available for download on GitHub. This model differs from traditional spin-1 Ising models due to the presence of a time-scale based interaction preference. The model's dynamics can switch between three states: the elimination of one species and the coexistence of the other two. Our research reveals that the dynamics favor the coexistence of both species over the elimination of one, although this trend can be disrupted by the right balance of interaction time-scales. Furthermore, we find that a species' persistence in a dynamic environment can be determined by its ability to survive on still, versus moving sites. In the process, we observe complex state transitions, driven by changes in the time-scale preferences, which can take the form of attracting fixed points, periodic oscillations, or chaotic behavior. These dynamics lead to the elimination of one species in a process that can become increasingly irregular, whereas the model's name'species elimination transition' captures its basic, stable nature. Our findings also demonstrate that the model can move beyond this core state by entering a state of species competition, known as the 'competition phase', where both species coexist and the model parameters create a complex, three-dimensional state space that is difficult to predict. This research introduces an novel integrated networking framework that brings together D2D communication, Energy Harvesting, and Integrated Information Theory. This framework, which we call IRIEN, enables two devices to connect with each other in a closed loop, converting previous electrical signals into new forms of energy and using that energy to power their connections. Our goal is to optimize the flow of information between the two devices and their energy harvesting capabilities. We then look at how this integrated system can be expanded to a group of devices and explore various ways to configure these groups of IRIEN connections. We also introduce an problem of great difficulty that involves finding the optimal IRIEN connection configuration for a specific scenario. We show that this problem can be rephrased as an instance of a well-known problem that can be solved using a specific algorithm, but we also prove that this algorithm has a significant drawback when dealing with large groups of devices. We then propose a much more efficient new algorithm that addresses this limitation, but our research falls short of fully analyzing this new algorithm and exploring its potential limitations. We also explore an alternative way of configuring these groups of IRIEN connections and identify a key optimization problem that can be solved using a more straightforward algorithm. We then test our proposed algorithm and this simpler solution using a simulated environment and compare them to the current state of the art. Our results show that both of our proposed solutions outperform the current standard, but we also acknowledge the significant gap in our research by emphasizing the need to further examine our proposed algorithm and explore its potential drawbacks. We believe that this research is significant because it brings together multiple disparate fields and explores their integrated potential, but we also recognize that there are many unanswered questions in this area. We hope that our work will guide and inform this broader research community and provide a foundation for further investigation and analysis. A single-point laser Doppler velocimeter (LDV) is typically limited to measuring velocity components along a straight line, intersecting a target with two perpendicular axes. This limitation can be circumvented by controlling the position of the LDV probe to match the orientation of the target's axes, enabling the collection of two-dimensional velocity data. This research presents several novel methods for automatically adjusting the LDV probe in three-dimensional space to determine the optimal orientation for maximum two-dimensional velocity component correlation. The most effective approach, the "paraboloid method", outperforms the others by utilizing the probe's orientation as additional variables in the correlation calculation. This results in the probe's optimal orientation being coincident with the target's axes, which can be precisely determined from the shape of a correlation paraboloid. Both theoretically and experimentally, the validity of this approach is demonstrated. We derive new conclusions regarding the transcendence degree of certain non-commutative extensions of the rational numbers. Specifically, given a polynomial $P$ of degree $d$ in $n$ variables and a multiplicative distribution $\omega$, we establish that the set of algebraic numbers encompassing the values of $\omega(P(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_n))$ has a maximum transcendence degree of $[d(n-1)]$ among the totally real algebraic numbers. This extends and generalizes a significant transcendence degree result originally proved by Leopoldt. Additionally, we provide a more nuanced statement for an arbitrary degree $n$ and any polynomial of degree $d$, incorporating a key requirement known as non-degeneracy. This non-degeneracy condition, coupled with further considerations, enables us to achieve an optimal transcendence degree of $n(d-1)$, surpassing the previously established bound from depth results by Kummer, Kronecker, and others. This research also yields analogous and innovative proofs for a broad range of classical and renowned results, including but not limited to Fubini extensions, generalised Hilbert's Seventh Problem, its various iterations, and the celebrated Navier-Stokes equations, among others. These celebrated results have numerous notable consequences, such as but not limited to the uniqueness of the rational number field, the prime factorization property of algebraic integers, and the absence of non-trivial algebraic relationships defining transcendental numbers like e and pi. These esteemed and valuable outcomes demonstrate the substantial impact and significance of our work. This research was conducted in collaboration with W. Ballanche, J. Fayon, and C. Mignard. Moreover, we outline a strategy for extending our primary result to a broader class of analytic functions, which in turn would enable us to further generalise our findings and expand upon the achievements of celebrated mathematicians like Baker, Wustholz, and their respective collaborators. This broader generalisation, however, is confined to the monic polynomial scenario and requires the presence of a non-degenerate second derivative as well as additional requirements known as super-transcendence, which together guarantee an optimal transcendence degree of $n(d-1)$ among the totally real algebraic numbers. This research also yields a significant depth result of $n(d-1)$, which in turn yields further depth results of $nd$, $nd+1$, and $nd+2$ as specific examples. These outcomes and their associated proofs can be found in the companion paper

In experiments involving particle collisions, a new, elastically coupling axion-like particle (ALP) can shine brightest at the level of missing energy. However, the effectiveness of this approach relies on the ability of detectors to accurately account for neutral particles that might interact with light. While such interactions are essential for the ALP's signal, they also cause the particle to escape undetected in certain cases. To address this, we evaluated the sensitivity of Belle II's detector at identifying ALPs produced in processes involving certain heavy mesons decaying into two photons. The results show that Belle II can efficiently detect ALPs in the majority of these cases but will often fail to do so for certain heavy meson decay modes. To enhance the discovery potential at Belle II, we recommend targeting production processes that are less likely to result in the ALP's disappearance. For the $B$ meson sector, the most promising approach involves looking for missing energy in conjunction with a single photon emitted at a large angle. Our findings suggest that Belle II can accumulate $10^{12}$ $B$ meson events, potentially leading to the creation of an accessible mass range for the ALP, down to $200$ MeV or less, subject to further calibration. To this end, we propose a data selection strategy that can significantly improve the detector's sensitivity to ALPs produced in $B$ meson decays. To facilitate similar analyses at other experiments, we have developed a comprehensive, publicly available tool that can simulate the production and detection of ALPs. This simulation takes into account various processes and interactions affecting the ALP's behavior and allows users to customize the output for multiple experiments involving different collision energies and detectors. To further optimize the discovery potential at Belle II, we recommend increasing the luminosity per bunch crossing or modifying the beam bunch structures. These changes, coupled with a more selective data selection strategy, have the potential to open up an extensive region of the parameter space for the ALP, potentially down to masses of $300$ MeV or less. To facilitate a better understanding of the results presented here, we have developed a set of numerical tools that can be accessed through a dedicated public webpage. These resources are designed to be accessible to a broad audience and can be used to explore the behavior of the ALP in various processes and interactions affecting its development and our ability to detect it. To a large extent, the development of these tools relied on the existing ALPPEG package, a public interface for the form factors calculated using the BaBaG code.

This paper provides an overview of using contextualized language frameworks, a significant development in natural language processing, that significantly boosts the performance of various NLP tasks. However, when applied to studying linguistic change, particularly diachronic research on semantic evolution and historical word sense evolution, these models have been found to have limitations. In our work, we employed BERT and other contextualized frameworks to analyze the nuances of language change and explored three related aspects of semantic evolution including syntactic expansion, lexical proliferation, and pejoration/amelioration. By extracting and annotating features from contextualized embeddings for a representative set of words exhibiting these changes, we gathered valuable insights into their patterns and potential pitfalls when studying language change with contextualized models. Ultimately, our research contributes to the growing body of literature on using contextualized language frameworks for diachronic research and offers a specific set of annotated data that other scholars can draw upon in their own studies. By exploring these findings and the associated limitations, we aim to guide other researchers through the features and potential pitfalls of contextualized models in their own studies of language change. A distinctive cellular movement called interkinetic nuclear migration occurs in
embryonic brains. This pattern of cell nucleus movement between the upper and
lower edges of the neuroepithelial tissue, alternating between individual cells,
enables proper organization of the brain by positioning neurons above and below
the developing cerebral surface. In this study, we utilize high-resolution three
dimensional imaging and analysis to examine this phenomenon in the developing
zebrafish retina. Retinal neuroepithelial cells display both interkinetic nuclear
migration and cell body oscillation patterns previously observed in the brain.
Surprisingly, we discover that both these patterns, common to all cells within
a particular retinal section, conform to a random or diffusive spread, unlike
the individual cell-based, deterministic model previously proposed. This study
further investigates the underlying factors influencing this migration, such as the
availability of the retinoic acid metabolite, all-trans retinoic acid, by
conducting both normal developmental and experimental analysis. Our findings
indicate that this migration pattern plays a crucial role in determining the
retinal tissue's overall structure and that it too is influenced by all-trans
retinoic acid, although this effect appears unlike its impact on brain tissue.
Ultimately, this study and its results provide a starting point for better
understanding both the development of the retina and the brain, given the
striking similarities observed between these two tissues. Given the widespread
occurrence of interkinetic nuclear migration, further research into this
phenomenon could also shed light on the development of multiple other tissues. A

website. A movie illustrating a particular retinal section's interkinetic

In this study, we develop an innovative codes' enrichment strategy, assigning distinct codes to specific categories that certain data points belong to. Our code-assignment approach ensures a good balance between code diversity and a particular criterion of choice, which is achieved by applying a weighted minimization of a LP-regularized problem. We demonstrate the versatility of this approach by applying it to two separate and independent applications: it enhances coding patterns that are beneficial for successfully reconstructing compressed images that were originally captured with a specific type of camera, and it facilitates efficient video matching through an index structure that can be compressively constructed. Code-assignment to a common basis allows us to adapt and refine our previous work on video matching, and to present a novel compressed image reconstruction technique that integrates spatial and temporal correlations. We test and evaluate our code-assignment strategy along with the two associated applications, and our results show the benefits of this strategy and its associated applications. Our code-assignment code is available for public use at https://github.com/username/Code-Assignment. Our compressed image reconstruction and video matching code are also available for public use at https://github.com/username/Compressive-Reconstruction-and-Matching. Our code-assignment approach can be applied to any problem that involves assigning data points to categories defined by different codes, as we have shown with our two test cases. However, we suspect that there are many other problems that our approach can also be applied to, given its universal nature. We encourage other researchers to try our approach on their own projects. Standard OCR tools, designed for high-density documents like the Indonesian ID, struggle with poor picture quality and varied font sizes. Presently, there are no established methods or scripts to automatically extract data from Indonesian ID documents. To address this issue, a document extraction process is proposed, beginning with an optical character recognition to generate a text-based document, followed by a natural language post-analysis to accurately obtain the desired information. A sample ID document from North Sumatra is used to demonstrate the effectiveness of this proposed method, which can be applied to other types of ID documents with some modification. The proposed technique provides a versatile framework for extracting data from various Indonesian ID documents, offering potential applications in fields like biometrics and secure transactions. The associated code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/ahmaddaudin/indonesian-id-document-extractor.

We show that any subgroup of diffeomorphisms with finite damage, as defined by Mjcikowski, Nekrashevych, and Swiencki, preserving the surface's boundary, does not have a precompact collection of subgroups when using the Roelcke metric. This contradicts a previous hypothesis proposed by Durcik and Mjcikowski. Additionally, we demonstrate that certain subgroups of $Homeo^+(S^1)$ are non-precompact in the uniform metric, expanding earlier results of Kahller, Mjcikowski, Nekrashevych, and Swiencki. This research also provides a new interpretation of a previous theorem by Mjcikowski and Nekrashevych. A key tool in our proof is a new property of groups with finite damage, specifically that they contain no copy of the group of rational numbers. This property is achieved by establishing an analogy between the surface's diffeomorphisms and the group of rational numbers in the context of the damage metric. This analogy enables us to apply results originally developed for the metric space of homeomorphisms, ultimately leading to our main hypothesis-shattering result. This research was previously a part of an unpublished manuscript from 2015. Note: After posting the preprint for this paper, we received helpful feedback from J. F. Brock, who pointed out that the hypothesis we were attempting to challenge was actually proposed by Durcik and Mjcikowski, not by Mjcikowski and Nekrashevych as previously stated. Additionally, we discovered that the property of surface diffeomorphisms with finite damage not containing the rational numbers was a well-established fact that can be found in the work of Mjcikowski and Nekrashevych. Moreover, we found that our proof of this property is a direct application of one of their theorems, and we have the permission from the editors of the Annals of Mathematics to use this established result in our paper. Similarly, we discovered that the property we called unique ergodicity is actually referred to as topological unique ergodicity in the literature, and we have the permission from the editors of the Annals of Mathematics to use this established result in our paper. Lastly, we found that we are not the first to consider the metric space of homeomorphisms with finite damage, and we have the permission from the editors of the Annals of Mathematics to use this established result in our paper. This research was supported in part by NSF

This research introduces a new category of computable functions known as regular string transformations, which are capable of taking infinite strings as input and producing transformed strings based on specified rules. Unlike acceptance procedures, these transformations don't have a predetermined output format. We identify two primary subcategories of regular string transformations: (1) those that generate output strings with a finite length, and (2) those that generate output strings with an infinite length. We further subdivide the latter category into two types: (2a) those that produce output strings with a well-ordered structure, and (2b) those that produce output strings with an arbitrarily complex structure. We demonstrate that first-order string logic is insufficient for expressing many of these string transformations and provide a more comprehensive framework called regular string logic. This new logic includes both input- and output-string definitions that can be decided by Turing machines with an infinite tape. We establish that (1) there are string transformations that can be defined using Turing machines but cannot be expressed in first-order logic, (2) these machines are unable to generate output strings with an arbitrarily complex structure, and (3) we have a rigorous time-complexity bound for determining whether a given string falls within a specified pattern. We also explore various undecidability results and demonstrate that both the original Post correspondence problem and the more general rational correspondence problem can be encoded as infinite string transformations. Additionally, we show that many of these transformations have a'simple' structure that can be expressed using a more primitive form of first-order string logic known as monadic string logic. This latter result involves a deeper analysis of (2a) the string transformations that produce output strings with a well-ordered structure and allows us to establish a 'twin' undecidability result among (1) the problem of determining whether a given string falls within a specified pattern, (2) the problem of deciding the validity of a given formula in the context of (1), and (3) the problem of determining whether a given string corresponds to a specified sequence of rules, as well as examining the relationship between these problems and other well-known problems of a similar computational complexity. This research further introduces a new problem of determining whether a given string corresponds to a specified sequence of rules, which we term the rational correspondence problem or RCP, as well as exploring its various forms and both direct and indirect relationships with other problems of a similar computational complexity. For a class of non-Newtonian fluids known as complex fluids, researchers have identified two distinct types of particles that interact with them - either attracting or repelling each other. Interactions of a particle with the fluid can be determined through force measurements during an experiment where the particle moves through the fluid. However, determining the interactions of a second particle with the same fluid requires an extremely lengthy and laborious process of repeating the entire experiment. In this study, we circumvent this lengthy process by focusing solely on the force the fluid exerts on the first moving particle as the second particle is placed in the mixture. By analyzing this force, we are able to infer the unknown particle's interaction with the same fluid. When the unknown interaction is a repelling force, we found a way to determine it precisely, and when it's an attracting force, we found an approximate method to figure it out. These findings apply specifically to two types of interactions - whether the particles repel or attract each other - and were discovered through analysis of forces measured during an experiment where a particle was moved through a mixture of water and glycerin. This research is important because it paves the way for reducing the time and effort required to study the interactions of complex fluids and offers a valuable tool that can be used in multiple fields such as studying the interactions of drugs with complex fluids, in the food industry, and in the study of biological cells. Notably, we were able to predict the unknown interaction of a drug with complex fluids and observed the same interaction of a sediment particle with the same fluid. This study provides concrete evidence that there are mixtures of complex fluids that have two distinct states of interaction - one where particles repel each other and another where they attract each other - and we were able to demonstrate this phenomenon with an experiment. This finding is significant because it's the first time such a state of coexistence has been observed and it has the potential to be explained by a theoretical prediction made earlier. This research offers multiple avenues for future study and we have outlined some of these possibilities. This study provides original knowledge that has never been published before and offers a clear and easy-to-follow explanation of the methods and results. This research received no external funding and was conducted in an entirely independent manner. To analyze complex, multi-agent, non-cooperative systems with significant disturbances, we developed a new dynamic programming method by utilizing a Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) equation of second order. This approach allows us to determine optimal control strategies for individual agents in a wide range of scenarios, including those with constraints, obstacles, and competing agents. Interestingly, our approach differs from traditional second-order HJI equations, which typically result from the analysis of a single agent with a controller, and provide a second-order derivative-based sensitivity for the value function. This distinction enables us to construct a control policy for each agent using the value function and its derivatives as input. As a consequence, this method offers greater generality and flexibility compared to first-order dynamic programming. As a proof of concept, we apply this method to a simple linear system and a non-linear double integrator system. Furthermore, this approach can be combined with a sampling-based method, model predictive control (MPC), by utilizing the value function as a guide to determine a near-optimal initial control policy for numerical solution algorithms. This combined approach yields a more efficient algorithm compared to standard MPC methods. All the pseudocodes for the proposed solution algorithm are provided in detail. This method and its associated pseudocodes have been validated through numerous simulation experiments. This research was published in the IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control in the year 2020 under the name "A Second-Order Achievable Sets Computation Method via a Cauchy-Type Variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs Equation" by J. Lygeris, A. Geidankin, and K. G. Voulgaris. A follow-up publication in 2021 titled "Efficient Solution Algorithm for a Nonlinear Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs Equation with Second-Order Derivatives" further optimized the solution algorithm of the HJI equation. This version of the algorithm was successfully applied to multiple nonlinear systems, including a complex multi-agent system with competing agents. This version was also integrated with MPC, and all the pseudocodes for the solution algorithm have been made publicly available on GitHub. This research has been featured in the IEEE Transactions on Automatic Control and the IEEE Control Systems Technology. A related open-source MATLAB tool called HJI Solver has been developed, which is capable of solving a broad class of Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equations and has been successfully applied to multiple nonlinear systems. We investigated the concept of animacy in ventral temporal cortex, utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging along with computational modeling. Our study discovered a distinct pattern of activity specifically related to perceiving intentional movements as being generated by animated agents, which we termed the "animacy structure." Our analysis revealed that the animacy structure is composed of distinct components that contribute differently to the representation of human-like and artificial animation, which can be explained by a computational model that simulates the integration of multiple features used to identify animacy. We demonstrated that the animacy structure is sensitive to the intentions behind movements, distinguishing between leading and following actions, and that it represents movement generation intentions that are distinct from action execution intentions. Notably, our findings showed that the animacy structure is more strongly represented in the temporal lobe when human rather than robot animation is presented, which can be attributed to the greater complexity of human movements that are influenced by a range of social cues, including facial expressions, postures, and body language. Our research into the animacy structure provides a framework for better understanding the neural mechanisms that give rise to the sense of agency and the animation of artificial entities, and has implications for the development of more realistic computer-generated human animation that accurately conveys the sense of agency and animacy. Furthermore, our results suggest that the temporal lobe's sensitivity to movement generation intentions can be a neural marker for the animacy structure, which can be exploited in a variety of applications including the detection of abnormal behavior in robotics and filmmaking. We discuss the potential of our model to be adapted for these purposes. The study on the animacy structure and its relationship to human and artificial animation presented here offers a significant contribution to the field of computer animation and robotics, which is supported by the numerical results obtained. This research builds upon the concept of quantum unique ergodicity, initially developed by Ludwig's work in 2010, particularly in the context of GL_2 Hecke-Maass forms. It demonstrates the universality of quantum unique ergodicity, showcasing that it is an ergodic property that arises when the geodesic flow on the moduli space of elliptic curves is nearly invariant under the action of the full 2-genius gallery. This finding holds when the Dirichlet series associated with these forms exhibit certain zero-free regions, and it extends the initial result by establishing the ergodicity of Landau-Siegel zeros. Additionally, it proves that there are no sequences of Landau-Siegel zeros that behave asymptotically, and this result shares some commonalities with Russell's recent work. Notably, this research does not rely on any conjectural hypotheses, and it establishes the ergodicity of the geodesic flow on the space of genus 1 surfaces with ramification, conditioned on the absence of Landau-Siegel zeros. This condition is necessary as the existence of Landau-Siegel zeros is incompatible with the phenomenon of quantum unique ergodicity. This finding can be achieved through the use of Selberg's delta function and its properties, along with the use of Poincaré series and their associated zeros. It also demonstrates that the ergodicity of the geodesic flow on the space of genus 1 surfaces with ramification is closely tied to the behavior of these functions, particularly in regards to the distribution of their zeros. It further shows that the distribution of these zeros is independent of the underlying geometric structure, and it shares some commonalities with the distribution of zeros from the Riemann zeta function, particularly in regards to the pair correlation function. This research examines the distribution of these zeros using a variety of methods, including the use of Selberg's delta function and its properties, along with the use of Poincaré series and their associated zeros, and it provides a more in-depth analysis of the distribution of these zeros, particularly in the context of the pair correlation function. It further examines the distribution of these zeros from multiple angles, and it provides a more in-depth understanding of the behavior of these functions and their associated zeros, along with the phenomenon of quantum unique ergodicity and its relationship to the distribution of these zeros. We have adapted the classical relational Hoare calculus for sequential programs to a quantum version, referred to as the quantum relational Hoare calculus for sequential programs, and established that this version is equivalent to the quantum approach using predicates and their related sound and complete proof system. The quantum relational Hoare calculus for sequential programs is expressed using pre- and post-relational assertions, where the relational assertion that results from program execution is uncertain and represented as a statistical measurement, known as an expectation value. We have also extended the quantum relational Hoare calculus to accommodate programs with non-deterministic components and demonstrated that this version is sound and complete. Furthermore, we have incorporated the quantum relational Hoare calculus into a proof system and demonstrated its effectiveness through a case study involving a simple quantum program. The case study illustrates how the quantum relational Hoare calculus handles program validity in a practical scenario. The potential for neural network-based extrapolation techniques to introduce biases in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in areas near sunspots, is a significant concern. Such biases could stem from the neural networks' limited training data or inherent properties and need to be identified in order to accurately apply these methods. We suggest a statistical approach to assess the neural network's performance and potential sources of bias, such as its influence on $\theta_c$ estimates. Our study reveals that despite the neural networks successfully inferring intensity profiles at multiple wavelengths, they introduce a systematic error in $\theta_c$ estimates near sunspots. We also find that these errors are more pronounced in areas with stronger magnetic fields and that there's a notable discrepancy in the neural networks' performance when comparing direct and indirect measurements. To address these issues, we propose two approaches: one is to combine the neural networks with a bias-correcting model based on an inverse problem, and the other involves using a genetic algorithm to train the networks on a more diverse set of sunspot data. We demonstrate that both methods can significantly reduce the biases and discrepancies found in the data. Our study highlights the importance of validating neural network performance, particularly in areas near sunspots, and in assessing their potential sources of bias in order to accurately apply these methods. We also emphasize that there's a need for high-resolution, detailed synthetic sunspot data to simulate and test these models effectively. Our proposed bias-correcting approaches are applicable to a broad range of neural network-based extrapolation techniques and provide a framework for evaluating and alleviating biases in vector magnetic field maps. Our results are relevant to any research involving the application of neural networks to infer missing intensity profiles and provide a foundation for further studies on the validation and effective use of these models. Our approach can be adapted for use in other research contexts, such as in the analysis of solar flare data, magnetic field maps, and in the validation of neural network-based models in astrophysics and other fields. Our proposed genetic algorithm training method can be a valuable tool for a wide range of applications in solar physics, astrophysics, and other fields that involve the analysis of complex, multi-dimensional data and provide a framework for validating and effectively using neural network-based models and other machine learning algorithms. A type of neural network known as complex-weight neural networks can automatically pick an appropriate time-reversal symmetry when training, which is particularly beneficial in addressing the "sign dilemma" problem that arises during the numerical solution of the Hubbard model using the interacting single-particle approximation. By analyzing a 1D Hubbard model, our complex-weight neural networks yield consistent and self-consistent results, even in situations where the electron-electron interaction is strong, by spontaneously breaking the time-reversal symmetry. This naturally occurring symmetry agrees with the one that would be arbitrarily chosen by the researchers if complex weights were employed. This inherent property of complex-weight neural networks, which was unexpectedly discovered in this study, can be a crucial advantage, as they are highly effective in overcoming the challenge of time-reversal symmetry breaking that is inherent in many research methods, not just the interacting single-particle approximation used here. This research is being published in Physical Review X. By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance a language model's cross-task generalization ability within an unsupervised framework, where the model acquires knowledge from a source domain to excel in a target domain. We introduce a retrieval-boosted method that harnesses unlabeled data from the target domain to fine-tune the model, successfully demonstrating improved performance on unsupervised cross-domain adaptations, including both simple and complex cases. When applied to a range of unsupervised inferences and a machine translation setting, our approach shows significant gains over baseline methods. The retrieved data's explicit exclusion of the source domain helps prevent domain contamination and allows the model to concentrate on the target domain. By inputting only the model's initial predictions on the retrieved data, we minimize the risk of overfitting and guide the model towards the target domain without explicit training. This approach is efficient, considering that it doesn't require task-specific training or large amounts of target data. We also explore the introduction of a simple regularization technique to further control domain contamination. Code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghruvoq/unsup-crg. With 6 out of 10 unsupervised SuperNatural tasks demonstrated improvement, our approach shows that unsupervised cross-task generalization is feasible and valuable, offering numerous possibilities for further development. This work is the first to combine the advantages of both dense and sparse cross-task training and presents a distinct set of unsupervised cross-task challenges, along with our solutions. This research also introduces the Natural Language Understanding's first fully unsupervised evaluation on the SimpleWiki domain. We hope that in the future this research will guide the development of more effective cross-task training methods within the supervised category. It is observed that traditional grid search methods may lead to overestimation of the model's accuracy due to the limited nature of the generated training data. It employs a gradient-based optimization method to adjust the hyperparameters while maintaining data privacy. We employed two statistical methods to analyze chemical data from the APOGEE-2 survey, uncovering the star formation histories and chemical enrichment of the Milky Way. By integrating two random draws, one representing the formation and destruction of globular cluster stars, and another for the destruction of thick disk stars, we constructed a model that could be applied to multiple stellar populations. Following this approach, notable patterns and discrepancies in the data became apparent, specifically with regards to metal-poor stars in the inner regions of the galaxy. Our analysis suggested that approximately 20% of the galactic disk's stars originated from a low-to-intermediate metallicity population that was destroyed in a major merger event. This finding is consistent with the "Classic Monet" model proposed by Minchev and Frenk (2010). Additionally, we found that approximately 30% of the galaxy's stars fall outside of established population categories, with many of these stars residing in the inner regions and possessing a chemical composition more extreme than typical globular clusters. These results have significant implications for our understanding of the galaxy's formation and evolution. For instance, they suggest that the Nucleus of the Milky Way may have a distinct chemical composition, with a higher abundance of elements formed by the explosion of massive stars than previously believed. Moreover, the presence of metal-poor stars in the inner regions indicates that the galactic bulge and the nucleus may have distinct formation histories. We encourage further investigation into this topic, possibly with the help of additional data, such as proper motions that can provide insights into the dynamics of the galaxy. We also propose the term "Galactic Nucleus" be limited to the extremely dense, metal-poor population found in the very center of the galaxy, rather than referring to the entire nucleated region. This term is analogous to the term "Galactic Bulge" which refers to the entire bulge population, not just the central, densely packed population. We ended the chapter by highlighting the significance of open questions in the field of chemical cartography and the valuable contributions that future surveys with higher proper motion precision, such as the Gaia-ESO survey, can make. We also discussed the potential of the APOGEE-2 survey in mapping the chemistry of the Magellanic Clouds, the satellite galaxies of the Milky Way. We concluded the chapter by emphasizing the incredible value of chemical cartography in guiding future observational efforts and providing a framework for analyzing and interpreting the data obtained from these observations. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of data from their devices and equipment, leading to opportunities for analyzing them to improve patient care. For example, analyzing oxygen levels in operating rooms can help identify areas for improving patient safety. However, processing large datasets efficiently enough to discover valuable patterns and trends within a short period of time, typically twenty-four hours, poses a significant challenge. To address this issue, we designed and implemented a data processing engine called LifeStream, which is specifically tailored to handle time-sensitive operations on large datasets and provides real-time results that can be acted upon within a day. LifeStream outperforms other state-of-the-art solutions by a factor of five, as demonstrated in our evaluation using real-world data from a hospital. Furthermore, we open-source LifeStream to facilitate its use in similar applications across the medical field. Moreover, we provide a case study on the efficacy of analyzing oxygen levels in operating rooms, leading to the discovery of potentially life-threatening situations and providing a foundation for conducting more in-depth research into this important topic. Lastly, we highlight a previously unreported issue with the Anesthesiologists' practice that we uncovered during this analysis.

This paper explores a specific type of curve, called a timelike Bertrand curve, existing within a semi-Euclidean space of three dimensions. We derive the differential equation that these curves must satisfy and identify several key properties they possess. Notably, it is demonstrated that the natural shadow of a timelike Bertrand curve in a three-dimensional Euclidean space is composed of line segments. This property is distinct from its counterpart in two-dimensional spaces, where the natural shadow is made up of arc segments. A special category of Bertrand curves, called regular Bertrand curves, is also examined and their properties discussed. A notable connection between regular Bertrand curves and geodesics in a hyperbolic space is established. All curves that satisfy the differential equation can be transformed into geodesics of a hyperbolic space with specific curvature characteristics. This relationship provides a new perspective on these curves and potentially serves as a platform for future analysis. A concrete example is given where we successfully integrate the differential equation and recover one of the previously identified solutions. This serves as an illustration of the hyperbolic geodesic scenario and its associated curve properties. A comment is also made on the integration challenge that arises when attempting to integrate the differential equation for curves in a four-dimensional semi-Euclidean space. This is in contrast to the earlier two-dimensional analysis where the differential equation could be directly integrated. A special category of Bertrand curves, called conformal Bertrand curves, is also introduced and its properties discussed. These curves have the distinctive feature of maintaining their angle in relation to a fixed line, regardless of the space they inhabit. A notable connection exists between these curves and the geodesics of a hyperbolic space, specifically de Sitter space. This relationship offers insights into and potential platforms for future analysis of these curves. A concrete example is given where we successfully integrate the differential equation and recover one of the identified solutions, demonstrating the hyperbolic geodesic scenario and its associated curve properties. This completes the analysis of Bertrand curves within the context of a hyperbolic space. A relevant question posed is whether these curves have a physical interpretation, and if so, what this interpretation might be. This paper also presents some open discussion on the subject of conformal Bertrand curves and their associated space, along with the integration challenge that arises when attempting to integrate the differential equation for curves in a four-dimensional semi-Euclidean space. Re-training deep learning models with an altered loss function is a common practice, and this approach is often linked to improving robustness and minimizing the impact of distributional shifts. Yet, the underlying reasons for how loss function modifications influence performance and model robustness remain poorly understood. This study aims to explore the effects of loss function alterations and their impact on the decision-making process during training. We utilize a simple neural network and a binary classification problem to illustrate and analyze the role of loss function modifications. Our results show that such modifications affect the model's ability to accurately determine the probabilities of each class. In essence, loss function alterations cause the model to become more conservative in its probability estimates by reducing its confidence. This, in turn, allows it to better resist distributional shifts and perform better in scenarios involving rejection. Notably, our findings challenge a widely held assumption related to the use of the softmax function in neural networks and their ability to provide probability estimates. We solve the Klein-Gordon equation using WKB approximations and apply the quantum-capability condition to the coefficients of the asymptotic expansion. The resulting modified Poisson-Schrödinger equation is used to analyze the properties of de Sitter spacetime. Within the context of this model, we examine quantum-capability indicators such as the quantum curvature parameter and spacetime compressibility. The occurrence of spacetime compressibility is linked to the emergence of quantum boundaries that coincide with horizons in specific situations, including black hole event horizons and cosmological horizons in de Sitter spacetime. The compressible regions of spacetime are characterized as quantum-capability regions that may have implications for the localization of quanta in these areas. The analysis of a spherically symmetric black hole event horizon reveals that the compressible region at the event horizon can extend to a distance three times the radius of the black hole, providing a quantum-capability signature that could aid in the identification and characterization of this region using LISA. The analysis of de Sitter spacetime Sp(2,R) gauge field theories also yields compressible regions at a distance of approximately three times the radius of the Sp(2,R) condensate, which may have observable effects on the cosmic microwave background. This comprehensive set of outcomes is analyzed to show that real-world outcomes generally fall into a limited number of categories, with just seven primary types. Our goal in creating this atlas of outcomes is to provide a structured framework for understanding the vast quantity of information in ATOMIC, setting it apart from more disorganized existing datasets of this kind. This atlas of outcomes is available for use in a variety of If-Then Reasoning applications, including but not limited to Text Classification, Machine Reading Comprehension, and Machine Question Answering. Our Quantum Approximate Simulations (QAS) framework, dubbed NISQ-HHL, focuses on efficiently mitigating performance issues in QAS, enabling reliable results on next-generation quantum machines. By optimizing portfolio configurations, NISQ-HHL accelerates approximate Hamiltonian simulation to the point where it can efficiently accomplish tasks beyond the reach of classical supercomputing. Concretely, our proposal yields a factor of 32 improvement in execution time and a 128-fold reduction in required qubit resources for a crucial Reagent Cycle simulation. If extended to the NISQ era, NISQ-HHL can achieve a 256-fold speedup and a qubit reduction factor of 64. Although primarily designed for QAS, NISQ-HHL's capabilities also make it suitable for executing a broad category of Hamiltonian-based quantum circuits. Nonetheless, its limitations in the quantum standard model await discovery. To move forward, we propose conducting an experimental investigation of NISQ-HHL using real quantum machinery. Specially, a study of QAS performance on a mock chemical reaction, along with an analysis of portfolio-driven simulations to a point where they intersect with the quantum standard model. This research was supported in part by IBM, ARO, and NSF. All corresponding pseudocode has been deposited at arXiv.org. Additionally, instructions for using NISQ-HHL with real quantum machinery are provided. Notably, NISQ-HHL's performance can be a "worst-case" outcome, and improving QAS generally should also lead to an improvement in NISQ-HHL. If executed, the proposed experimental investigation of NISQ-HHL would entail approximately $10^9$ gate credits. This article uses combinatorial methods to analyze the asymptotic properties of a specific point set called "uniform parking functions". A set of points in a higher dimensional space is considered uniform if it results from the superimposition of several hypercubes with their lower left corner at the origin, orientated randomly. The term "hypercubes" refers to higher dimensional equivalents of square boxes. To generate the set of uniform parking functions, a random process is applied to each of these hypercubes. The process, known as the "raising function" or "ascending order statistic", sorts the points within each hypercube based on their distance from the origin. A type of exotic baryon called $\Omega^{-}$ has been theoretically predicted with properties that deviate from normal physics laws, displaying "CBM" behavior when subjected to strong magnetic fields. Although this baryon has an elusive nature and has been infrequently detected in laboratory experiments. The present study aims to explore the possibility of detecting it using heavy-ion collision data at the STAR experiment located at RHIC, with 200 GeV collision energy, with $\Omega^{-}$ formed in central Au+Au collisions then tracked in magnetic fields of varying intensities. A sophisticated algorithm was developed to identify $\Omega^{-}$ based on their distinctive weak decay into kaons, with over 6 million events analyzed from an 11-week data set. The study focuses on the 1.04 GeV energy range, accessible through the subsequent decay of $\Omega^{-}$, specifically looking at $\Lambda$ (1396 MeV) with large angular moment, which can provide insights into $\Omega^{-}$ properties and the "CBM" effect, as well as offering a means to validate the $\Omega^{-}$ identification method used. The resulting data allows for a detailed examination of $\Omega^{-}$ properties, through complex magnetic field effects on its weak and electric charges, which could be compared to theoretical predictions made possible by the detection of $\Omega^{-}$. The study also outlines potential paths for improving the $\Omega^{-}$ detection efficiency, which could be relevant for similar experiments at lower collision energies, such as the HADES experiment with 2.9 GeV collision energy, with SPS and LHC experiments at 17.3 and 13 GeV collision energies offering less suitable conditions for detecting it. The findings presented here are from 2017 and 2018 data sets, with subsequent years offering improved $\Omega^{-}$ detection efficiency. The study provides a starting point for further studies into the $\Omega^{-}$ properties and the "CBM" effect, which could be relevant for a wide range of heavy-ion collision experiments. The data used in this study has been made available through the RHUL neutrino group's interactive neutral meson production page, which offers access to similarly processed neutral meson collision data, as well as raw experimental data suitable for independent analysis, with related theoretical predictions available through the JAM code, which is also suitable for independent analysis with detailed guidance available. The study has implications for experimental designs at heavy-ion collision facilities, which could benefit from adding detectors capable of observing rare baryons like $\Omega^{-}$.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like public transportation is intricately affected by various physical phenomena, particularly the behavior of aerosols, respiratory patterns during breathing, talking, and coughing, and how viruses spread from an individual to another through respiratory droplets.  Since this complex dynamics isn't well understood, different researchers have approached and analyzed these interactions in distinct ways. Some have used simple mixing models that aren't supported by experimental evidence, while others have used more detailed and scientifically-backed methods to examine superspreading events. This paper aims to explore how different models, including a proposed new air exchange-based framework, can capture the reality of urban bus environments. It also seeks to explore if more sophisticated models are better at predicting when and how illnesses spread among passengers. To achieve this, it uses a combination of experimental data from respiratory droplet spray tests, as well as a computational simulation of the same bus environments.
