This research investigates the spin-orbit proximity effect in layered structures composed of nonmagnetic Bi and ferromagnetic Co layers. By conducting a GGA+SO calculation, we examined the magnitude of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in individual Bi layers and at interfaces, as well as how it influences the magnetic properties of Co layers. It was discovered that the magnitude of SOC in the Co layers depends on whether they are situated near a interface or in the interior of the structure. Furthermore, we found that the magnetic properties of the Co layers are affected by the presence of Bi layers due to the spin-orbit proximity effect, enabling us to explore potential applications in, for example, spin-orbit coupled systems and racetrack memories. To accurately predict their operational characteristics, we conducted a $k\cdot p$ calculation for a simplified model consisting of a free electron layer at a Bi/Co interface. This model allows us to analyze the operating principles of devices that utilize the spin-orbit proximity effect, spin-orbit coupling, and Landau levels. It was discovered that the interplay between the magnetic field, electric field, and the interface's spin-orbit coupling can result in operating modes for devices that rely on the spin-orbit proximity effect, landau levels, and elastic backscattering. To further analyze these devices, we conducted a $k\cdot p$ calculation for a more complex model featuring a narrow free electron layer sandwiched between two Bi layers and a Co layer. This more advanced model enables us to investigate the effects of the free electron layer's filling factor on the magnitude of the spin-orbit coupling and the elastic backscattering, which in turn affects the operating modes of the devices. It was discovered that the interaction between the electric field, the interface's spin-orbit coupling, and the free electron layer's filling factor can influence the magnitude of the spin-orbit coupling and elastic backscattering, and as a result, the operating modes of the devices are highly sensitive to any alterations made to these conditions. This robust mechanism of the spin-orbit proximity effect, combined with the free electron layer's narrowness and the associated landau levels, presents an innovative approach to controllably design and operate devices that rely on the interaction between the magnetic field, the free electron layer's filling factor, and the interface's spin-orbit coupling, and as such, has far-reaching implications for the advancement of the field. We introduce a novel neural network architecture that combines two separate images, one with a high dose and one with a low dose, to generate a high-quality low-dose PET image. This architecture, which we call DOPED, incorporates several innovative features to ensure it can handle both training and test data effectively. Firstly, DOPED incorporates a physics-based noise model to better capture the characteristics of PET images. Secondly, this model includes an uncertainty estimation component to determine the confidence of its outputs. Thirdly, we develop a robust training method for DOPED called Physically Aware Noise Regularized Optimization. Finally, to accommodate out-of-distribution data, we modify the architecture to output multiple images along with their corresponding confidence levels. We validated the DOPED model using low-dose PET data from four different scanners and found it outperformed state-of-the-art baseline models in terms of image quality and accuracy. Additionally, our results showed that the DOPED model can reduce the dose of PET scans to 1.25 Mbps (from the original 10 Mbps) while maintaining comparable image accuracy. To further analyze the DOPED model's performance, we created a subset of PET images that were intentionally degraded to mimic real-world scanning scenarios and found that this model performed consistently well across all such scenarios. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/alberto-sangjoon/DOPED. We believe that the DOPED model has significant potential for clinical use in reducing PET scan doses. Moreover, our noise model and training data analytics can be utilized by the imaging community to better understand and improve PET image reconstruction techniques. We propose several future research directions for the DOPED model, including evaluating its performance on actual patient data, comparing it with baseline models using quantitative metrics, and adapting it for use with whole-body PET images. We also outline possible modifications to the DOPED model, including incorporating prior image information, developing a 3D version of the model, and creating a data modulator that mimics the effects of scattering in PET images. We believe that the DOPED model and our proposed research directions have significant value to the scientific community. We emphasize that our code is designed to be modular, allowing easy integration of new features and models. This connection holds true across different tasks and models, including BART. Recently, wireless networks have seen a significant surge in their use for estimating people's physical ranges, a task that is critical in various scenarios including security, navigation, and tracking. Fingerprinting techniques, which compare measured readings to those collected in advance, have become a popular method for range estimation in various environments using different technologies including WiFi, GPS, and Bluetooth. However, the effectiveness of these techniques depends heavily on building an accurate database of reference points, which can be both time-consuming and expensive to build, as well as a number of other factors including the accuracy of the device, the mobility of the people being tracked, and the density of the network used for the readings. In this research, we present a novel approach that leverages artificial intelligence through a multi-layer perceptron neural network to estimate the physical range of people using only a single WiFi device without the need for building a comprehensive database of reference points. The proposed system's dependence on such a database makes it both cost-efficient and simple to set up. Additionally, we provide a working demonstration of the proposed system using ESP32 devices and OpenCV. Experimental results using a WiFi-based range estimation system showed that it can estimate distances accurately, with a mean absolute error of  $23.5$  centimeters when the devices are moving and $13.5$  centimeters when they are stationary. These findings provide a solid foundation for applying the system in a variety of scenarios including navigation and security. The proposed system's simplicity and cost-effectiveness also make it an attractive option for use in the development of intelligent applications for the Internet of Things. The beam disruption effect poses a challenge for particle accelerators that involve the simultaneous acceleration and deceleration of charged particles. This issue affects energy recovery linacs negatively by contributing to the growth of unwanted oscillations in particle beams. The beam disruption interaction can result in non-linear effects that influence the macroscopic oscillations and, as a result, the stability of the system. Studies on beam disruption usually consider a single beam or a non-circulating electron beam. In contrast, our research examines the impact of beam disruption in an energy recovery linac with multiple filled bunches, focusing on a particular instability known as beam disruption instability. Our analysis reveals that the fill configuration significantly affects the level of instability and that properly aligning the beam packets within a bunch cage can substantially reduce the effects of beam disruption instability. This finding, combined with the results from our previous studies on emittance, suggests that energy recovery linacs with a specific fill configuration may have a greater potential for achieving optimal performance. Our numerical data illustrates the relationship between the alignment of charged particles, beam disruption instability, and the level of oscillation in a demonstration lattice for an energy recovery linac. This research investigates the fundamental process in which an additional gluon is emitted in the one-loop order within $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory when a pair of colorless scalar fields interact through a vertex at their center. The underlying theory's inherent properties simplify the calculation of this process, allowing it to be reinterpreted in terms of a three-point correlation function that can be analyzed using its own set of physical parameters. As a result, we derive the one-loop correction to this three-point correlation function, a key quantity that has never before been calculated in $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang-Mills theory. This finding has significant implications for a related conjecture made by Alday and Maldacena, and it provides a crucial test of this proposed duality. Moreover, we outline a method for extending this calculation to higher loop orders. This research also sheds light on the fundamental process of graviton emission in the one-loop order within $\mathcal{N}=4$ supergravity theory, a process that can be reinterpreted in terms of a four-point correlation function. The behavior of long, flexible polymer bristles under tension has been extensively studied and is well understood when the bristles are straight or curved in a sinusoidal pattern. However, the impact of localized constraints on shaped bristles, such as a surface-bound polymer, is less clear. In this work, we demonstrate that stretched bristles of any two-dimensional shape can be modeled using a network of entangled polymers, and that the tension within these bristles decreases exponentially with distance from their free ends. We also show that the stretching of bristles embedded in a surface can become resistant to deformation, creating an "exclusion area" that is bounded by a circular shape that is proportional to the square of the length of the bristle. This finding builds on previous research by removing the restriction that the excluded area must be a perfect circle, and provides the first demonstration of an excluded area in bristles that are bent into a non-linear shape. It also shows that bristles that are bent into a looped or curved shape can exhibit cooperative motion when pulled gently. This work was conducted using computational modeling of polymer bristles, with the specific example of bristles bound to a surface being used to demonstrate the excluded area phenomenon. The metric dimension of a graph measures the minimum number of nodes required to identify all other nodes uniquely through distances. We introduce a new parameter, called the shortened metric dimension, which accounts for the number of nodes that can be directly seen from node transmissions in addition to distance-based identification. We examine key properties and possibilities for bounds on shortened metric dimension in various types of graphs, and establish a fundamental inequality showing that the shortened metric dimension can exceed the metric dimension by any given integer. Additionally, we provide specific examples and contrast them with general guidelines to demonstrate how the shortened metric dimension is affected in different graph configurations. Finally, we discuss possible approaches for investigating further results and offer a connection to an existing problem in Ramsey theory. All original proofs are included in the paper. We employed a large-scale artificial neural network to quickly process nearly a decade's worth of data from the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope Atlas, resulting in a concise and precise record of celestial events observed in the sky. By incorporating a sophisticated interpolation technique, we refined the atlas to better suit research requirements, accounting for sources whose radiation patterns shift over time, and identifying those that exhibit such variability. Our analysis suggests that around 7% of the sky's sources demonstrated radiation pattern changes, and 24% showed signs of temporal variability in their radiation, both of which could be explored further with additional data analysis. We intend to make our processed atlas available to the scientific community for future reference. Moreover, our research methodology offers a starting point for similar studies of varying duration datasets from the telescope. We also outline a method for identifying directed variability in sources, which could be valuable for identifying sources emitting pulsed signals. All-sky charts and detailed source records are accessible via an interactive online platform. We encourage users to verify our findings and contribute to future research by analyzing the data together. With this collaboration, we could tackle a wide range of tasks, including locating sources that emit polarized radiation, studying the properties of blazars, and analyzing data from the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer. In a sequence of independent first-price auctions where each auction's winner becomes the next period's "status" holder, having the highest valuation for the current period's auction is not sufficient to guarantee the maximum final period payoff. In fact, there may exist an over-serial dictatorship where the highest valued player has the lowest payoff in each period. We show that, when adding one auction to a serial dictatorship, the resulting payoff configuration can indeed be any convex combination of the individual period payoffs, except when there are three players with distinct valuations. Additionally, determining the added-auction payoffs that maximize the median of the payoffs is NP-hard. A key tool for our analysis is a newly introduced "project" function that helps analyze sequences of auctions. In a broader context, our research relates to a prior study on auction sequences by Krishna and Weber (2011) and extends the "project" function to its "expectation" form, enabling us to examine the optimal strategy for a single auction as well. This extension is relevant to a prior finding by Bikhchandani, Mookerjee, and Sontauk (2009) concerning the risk premium in a "herd" model. Our work also offers a sequential interpretation of the results presented in a prior study by Krishna and Weber (2011). Moreover, we offer two appendices that provide further details on the "project" function and the herding model risk premium. Sincerely, Kalyan Chawla and Soberman. Last revised Mar 25, 2023. We designed a sophisticated approach to pinpoint contact binary asteroids within specific orbits and investigate their overall population. A distinguishing feature of these binaries is their steady, nearly symmetrical orbital movement, causing their components to gradually drift apart over time. As a result, we can identify potential targets by tracking asteroids with irregular shapes that exhibit small, non-axisymmetric light variations across different images. Over time, those with binary orbits would exhibit changing light patterns as they rotate, despite maintaining an overall irregular shape. We developed a statistical model to account for any shape changes independent of rotation period, thereby focusing on those with pattern changes over time. To test this approach, we created a sample of known contact binaries with sufficient data to allow us to test our method and made it public. Then we applied our technique to Pan-STARRS1 images of nearly 150,000 asteroids across the inner solar system, covering orbits visible from the Sun's right side. From this analysis, our algorithm generated a vast list of potential binary targets awaiting further confirmation as actual binaries, with many being shaped by recent tidal disruptions that could provide valuable insights into binary evolution. Specifically, we found a binary population likely formed through gravitational scattering by the Sun, particularly in the inner regions, where many binary asteroids have orbits with high eccentricities and large axial tilts. These findings are consistent with recent studies and our estimates indicate that about 0.5% of asteroids with diameters over 100 km in the Sun's right hemisphere have binary orbits, shaped by the Sun's gravitational influence. These findings highlight the significance of binary asteroids as a critical component of our solar system's dynamic evolution and demonstrate the effectiveness of this novel approach in uncovering these binaries, with implications for similar searches using image data from other surveys. With access to complete orbital information, our technique can also provide valuable insights into the physical properties of these binaries, such as their component masses, allowing us to test theories of binary evolution and migration, and providing a valuable resource for future studies of the solar system, in particular its dynamic evolution through scattering and migration. A comprehensive database of our findings is available online. A subset of these targets will also be suitable for further confirmation using other observational methods, such as astrometry and spectroscopy, which can provide more detailed information about these binaries, with many offering valuable scientific opportunities, given their accessible orbits. We introduce the GPT-3 based model, known as AI Dungeon Master, which guides players through immersive text-based adventures like Dungeons and Dragons. AI Dungeon Master's interactions are organized around the player's intentions, which the model can identify, and it uses a simplified "theory-of-mind" to anticipate their next move. In response, it crafts a challenging and thematically appropriate scenario. To train this model, we created the Intent Theory-of-Mind in Dungeons and Dragons dataset, consisting of 20 different dungeons with multiple layers, covering both simple and complex social interactions, combat, and puzzle-solving. A key feature of this dataset is the presence of hidden intentions that players must uncover to progress through the adventure. Evaluations using both an automated system and human players demonstrate the model's capacity to engage in dynamic, purposeful conversations that meet their needs, providing a comprehensive framework for creating interactive stories and leading them towards a desired outcome. All necessary code and datasets for replicating this work are available at https://github.com/nytimes/ai-dungeon.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their functional flexibility is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research suggests that protein knots may not always be rigid structures, and some may have inherent tendency to bend and curve. A new topological approach is proposed that enables the detection of a protein's knotted surface and the identification of potential bending pathways through it. This method was applied to a subset of knotted proteins and revealed that their surface bending modes often intersect with the protein's core. Interestingly, when all knotted proteins are compared, distinct patterns of surface bending emerge that are specific to each knot type and cannot be explained by geometry alone. It is suggested that these patterns could be influenced by the molecular forces holding the protein together and that this could be determined using advanced molecular simulations. If this is possible, it would grant scientists access to the underlying physics governing the protein's knotted and curved state, and perhaps even provide a way to predict the knots and curvature of an unknown protein based on its genetic sequence. A hypothetical approach is outlined for how this could be achieved. It is also proposed that a more general "topological map" could be created that charts the possible bending and curvature of a protein's surface, and could be a valuable tool for biologists studying protein knots and protein function and evolution. It is shown that this map would have a simple and intuitive design, and would be capable of distinguishing between different types of knots and knots that are similar but not the same. It is also demonstrated that the complexity of a protein's knotted structure could be quantified, and that this measure correlates with the degree of curvature in the protein's surface and the number of different bending pathways it has. It is further proposed that advanced simulations could be used to examine the forces holding a protein together and the patterns of its surface bending, and it is shown that this could provide a precise and unbiased way of determining the physics governing a protein's knotted and curved state, and could be a valuable approach for predicting the knots and curvature of an unknown protein based on its genetic sequence. It is also shown that the complexity of a protein's knotted structure could be a reliable indicator of its functionality and how it evolves over time, and it is proposed that the study of protein knots and their complexity could be a valuable area of research for biologists and could provide new insights into the genetic code and the fundamental laws of physics and evolution. It is further proposed that the study of protein knots could be a valuable way of testing the accuracy of genetic sequence prediction algorithms

A detailed investigation of a specific type of Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem applies to relativistic quantum field theories, demonstrating that a lack of full symmetry in a Lagrangian density $\mathcal{L}$ in $\$(d+1)$\ dimensional spacetime inevitably leads to a vast number of NG bosons. This extension of a fundamental theorem, first proposed by Nambu and Goldstone, arises from the requirement that any consistent quantization procedure must maintain Lorentz invariance, despite the breaking of symmetry in the Lagrangian density $\mathcal{L}$. Consequently, a long-standing conjecture related to the number of NG bosons and their respective helicities is disproved. This unusual result implies that a general proof of the NG theorem cannot be achieved within the framework of perturbative quantum field theory. Notably, an analogous principle of the NG theorem also applies to nonrelativistic quantum field theories, extending its validity across different symmetry breakings. This work examines the number of NG modes and their corresponding helicities in both relativistic and nonrelativistic theories. It also discusses various examples of symmetry breaking, including a $U(2)\times U(1)$ nonabelian gauge theory and its relationship to the standard model of particle physics. A comparison is made with the little Higgs mechanism of particle physics, which relies on a different type of symmetry breaking known as "collective mode". A detailed analysis of the number of NG modes and their helicities in both relativistic and nonrelativistic versions is presented. This work paves the way for a better comprehension of the little Higgs mechanism and collectively charged modes in both the standard model and its various extensions, as well as in any other context in which this type of symmetry breaking contributes to the particle physics phenomenon. It also highlights the unusual nature of the NG theorem's applicability to both the relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories. A discussion of the possible consequences of this unusual result for any consistent quantization procedure and the little Higgs mechanism that arises from it is provided. A list of the NG modes and their helicities for both the relativistic and nonrelativistic theories is presented in tables S.I-X in the supplement. This work offers an accessible and in-depth examination of the NG theorem and its applications to both the relativistic and nonrelativistic quantum field theories, as well as to the little Higgs mechanism of particle physics. This work focuses on identifying the dimension of these codes, establishing that their dimension can be determined by examining the image of the generating matrix from the additive group of $\Z_{p^2}$ compared to its projection on $\Z_p$. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the dimension of these codes is directly related to the dimension of another code, described as a single-layered code defined over $\Z_p$. The paper also examines the null space of these codes and establishes that its basis consists of words with a particular $p$-adic expansion. This expansion indicates a distribution of the locator coefficients among the coordinates of the code, providing a means to determine the dimension of the code, in addition to identifying a subcode defined as $p$-fold self-parallel with a specified generator matrix. The relationship between this subcode and the original $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear code is then established, enabling the recovery of the original code from the subcode. The results presented can be applied to create an algorithm for determining the minimum distance of $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes, an achievement that was previously thought unattainable due to the complexity of calculating the Kronecker class of the code. Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in addressing the imbalance issue in data sets with a significant class imbalance. However, the training process for conditional GANs is known to be unstable and difficult to tune. In our research, we take a different approach and generate data based on a single positive example per class. We propose a method called "Single-Example Generation per Class" or SEGC, which employs a discriminator that identifies whether an instance and its corresponding label combination is genuine. We found that SEGC enables more freedom in data distribution compared to conditional GANs. As a result, we are able to generate labeled data with diverse attributes even when the original data set contains only a single positive example per class. We successfully apply SEGC to two such cases : generating synthetic data for imbalanced classification and combating multi-label instance generation constraints. Our experiments show that SEGC outperforms existing approaches in both scenarios. We are able to generate synthetic data with complex attributes and demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on five different data sets when comparing against conventional methods used for training models with multiple labels. We also show that SEGC can generate labeled data with diverse attributes even when the original data set contains only a single positive example per class. This is shown through an intuitive illustration and additional experimental results on the quality of generated data. We make public the code and guidelines for both SEGC and the baselines used in our research. This enables transparent verification of our findings and facilitates easy adoption of the proposed approach by the research community. This research is published open-source in the form of a long version of the paper. This long version includes background information, stone-age thoughts, detailed discussion of the proposed approach, the experimental framework used, the outcomes of the experiments, as well as the knowledge-related abstract used to guide the proposed approach. This long version of the paper is accompanied by supplementary materials that include additional results from the experiments, the hyperparameter tuning used for both the baselines and the proposed approach, the code for both the baselines and the proposed approach, the guidelines for both the baselines and the proposed approach, the outcomes of the experiments, and the discussion of the research. Quantum mechanics is often represented using Hilbert spaces as the primary structure, from which various other mathematical constructs can be derived, including, for instance, the algebra of observables. Conversely, certain approaches, such as the Dirac-Von Neumann construction and the Boehme-Schrader method, enable us to reconstruct a Hilbert space from a given algebra of observables. We establish that these two processes are systematically related and form part of a specific type of categorical relationship called an adjunction, specifically within the realm of 2-categories. This 2-category adjunction then serves as the fundamental framework for another related structure known as the Stone-Weyl theorem. Another significant finding arises from applying this framework to identify a specific type of algebraic structure associated with the set of status operators, which are used to investigate the properties of a quantum state. This specific algebraic structure is found to be equivalent to the algebra of functions associated with a compact, abelian group, for which we can determine a specific parametric representation. This representation can be further simplified by utilizing a particular subgroup associated with the set of status operators, which are defined as the operators that commute with the Hamiltonian of a harmonic oscillator. This specific group of status operators can be rigorously established as a Pauli group, for which we can determine its explicit parameters in a compact and simplified form. This finding provides the basis for analyzing the symmetries of a particular type of quantum state known as number states, which are defined as the energy eigenstates of a harmonic oscillator. This discussion on number states arises from the more general discussion on the relationship between the status operators, the algebra they form, and the associated group of symmetries, which we believe to be an essential and innovative contribution to the field. The precise origin of gamma-rays above 100 TeV in some nearby radio galaxies remains a mystery. The detection of steady, multi-TeV gamma-ray emission from three galaxies - M87, NGC 1068, and IC 761 - is a challenge to their existing theoretical frameworks. We propose an explanation for these observations involving accretion disks that are trapped by a magnetic field within the galaxies' centers. As matter is drawn into the supermassive black hole at the center, it creates a massive disk that generates both optical and X-ray radiation, while the trapped electrons emitting gamma-rays through the Bethe-Heitler process, also produce a gamma-ray peak in the high-energy range that is observable. To support this theory, we conducted simulations that replicated the disks' properties and accounted for the galaxies' varying optical and X-ray characteristics. By modeling the electrons' behavior and the effects of interstellar gas, our research found that it could replicate the observed gamma-ray ranges in M87, NGC 1068, and IC 761, offering a new perspective on these enigmatic objects and the physics governing their behavior.

This paper categorizes heart sounds based on three types of conditions: mitral valve issues, aortic valve issues, or combined problems. To achieve this, we considered two types of distortions associated with the recording process: additive noise and signal transformation. With these challenges in mind, we analyzed and presented a new approach that incorporates two main components: a deep neural network called a Residual Dense Network, which extracts features from the data, and a custom network that accounts for the physical recording environment to mitigate the effects of signal transformation and additive noise. To train and evaluate this model, we used a dataset from a specific recording device, and to ensure the results are applicable across different devices, we tested it on a dataset from a different manufacturer with similar valve condition combinations but with different types of valve problems. The model's effectiveness in both cases is demonstrated by its high accuracy in categorizing the heart sounds. This work paves the way for a physical and recording-condition-aware approach to analyze heart sounds, and the code is available online for further development. This model achieved an accuracy of 94.12% for mitral valve issues, 92.67% for aortic valve issues, and 91.54% for combined problems in the first dataset, and 92.33%, 89.52%, and 91.11% in the second dataset respectively. The models' performance can be improved by using more comprehensive training datasets, as the current limitation hinders its ability to generalize to a wider range of recording conditions and valve problem combinations. This study classifies and examines various portfolio optimization methods with higher order moments, including skewness and kurtosis, in finance. We review and analyze many approaches that consider the presence of asymmetry and tail heaviness to model non-Gaussian portfolio returns. The study categorizes these methods into four main groups based on their mathematical framework: utility theory, optimization with constraints, multi-objective optimization, and robust optimization. This paper discusses the evolving nature of software, illustrating how automated systems can progress from simple scripts to sophisticated applications requiring human intervention. A detailed examination is presented of a particular type of software called "malware," which is designed to deceive automated detection methods. In contrast to conventional threats, "advanced persistent threats" (APTs) use intricate techniques to evade discovery. A hypothetical scenario is described where a university student is suspected of uploading malicious software to the institution's network. This case serves as a model for how investigators use manual methods to analyze and identify malware, including using memory dumps to reconstruct the student's actions and prove guilt. A more efficient way to achieve this is proposed, using automated tools to streamline the investigation process. This problem is used to illustrate the challenges faced by APTs and other sophisticated software, which are designed to remain undetected for prolonged periods. A proposed solution is presented, involving the development of an automated proof system that can detect and validate the correctness of software, even when based on complex algorithms used in APTs. This is made feasible by reinterpreting the Pease-Assri program correctness proof method to accommodate the needs of this problem, where software correctness is validated through the reconciliation of multiple conflicting narratives. This new interpretation enables the use of program correctness proofs from various sources, including open-source applications, which can be combined to derive a general validity theorem. This theorem in turn can be used to develop an automated system for validating the correctness of software, even when based on complex algorithms used in APTs. This proposed system differs from conventional automated tools, which rely on the accuracy of their own programming without the need for input from external sources, providing a new perspective on the challenge of developing trusted automated systems, which are capable of making decisions based on human input,, and the efficacy of which is supported by the results of this research, which successfully detected and exposed the malicious intent of the student in the described scenario. We've analyzed a vast dataset of 21-cm neutral hydrogen emission and far-infrared spectral lines from 168 galaxies with a wide range of luminosities, primarily drawn from surveys with comprehensive coverage of the sky. By focusing on two key fine-structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, we discovered a straightforward linear relationship when comparing their brightness to that of hydrogen, with a specific constant factor. This constant factor holds a significant potential for use in studying the interstellar medium of galaxies, specifically regarding the gas temperatures and densities, given the low brightness of these lines relative to their extensive coverage of the sky and observations. Furthermore, this approach may provide a more direct and less biased approach in comparing gas temperatures and densities in galaxies, offering insights that modified black-body models, often used in far-infrared spectroscopy, may miss due to an over-reliance on assumptions about the spatial distribution of molecular gas and its associated temperatures. We've made the raw data and analysis code available openly, along with a simple model that can be used for comparing the brightness of the two C I lines, and have suggested future observations that may further explore our findings. This article examines a stochastic speed process derived from Type-A Non-Uniform Exclusive Process (ASEP), which differs significantly from its traditional counterpart. Contrary to the typical model, where each particle has a distinct speed, this new process involves particles moving at the same speed. However, they are restricted by partial exclusion rules. We establish that despite these differences, the one-site marginal probabilities of this stochastic speed process converge to the same stationary distributions as those obtained from the traditional ASEP model, where each particle has a unique speed. We also investigate the stationary properties of this stochastic speed process, revealing that its site-specific velocity distribution can be determined directly from its hydrodynamic equation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that its stationary currents are conserved and influenced by a specific boundary condition, which acts as a "source" or "sink" depending on the context. This leads to an interesting interpretation where the process can be seen as a second-order process, similar to the one observed in the traditional ASEP model. We end our analysis by applying these results to a specific context, an open system with a gradient, and comparing it to a closed system. This particular example involves a stochastic speed process at equilibrium, where the speed of each particle varies randomly. Notably, we find that its stationary velocity distribution can be obtained from its inviscid shock front equation, even though this process is discrete and stochastic in nature. This finding is particularly relevant as it provides a solution to a problem that has been previously mentioned in the works of Bernoullis, Hahn, and Levermore. We also offer a new and distinct proof for this distribution, which can be compared to the existing methods of proof presented in their work. This includes a combinatorial approach using the ASEP, as well as other methods, and a continuous approach using the Weakly Asymptotic Coupling (WAC) algorithm, among others. This particular context and its results can also be applied more broadly, offering a framework for analyzing similar stochastic speed processes in other settings. This study examines various mathematical models used to analyze epidemiological data during the COVID-19 pandemic. By reviewing 1,676 research papers on the subject, we explore how different models were applied to understand and predict pandemic trends. Epidemiological models were categorized based on their ability to incorporate multiple transmission dynamics, population characteristics, and geographical divisions. We evaluated the widespread use of ordinary differential equation-based models, agent-based models, network-based models, and other approaches such as discrete mathematical and computational models. Notably, we found a substantial increase in research on optimal control strategies and interventions. However, there's a growing need for more realistic and complex models that accurately capture diverse local pandemic patterns. With a significant portion of the world's population remaining unvaccinated, there's also a critical necessity for better understanding and modeling of long-term pandemic dynamics. We propose a new research direction focused on integrating models with publicly available data and forecasting tools to anticipate post-vaccination epidemiological trends. A hypothetical model for this purpose is presented, offering a framework that can be tailored to suit various global and regional pandemic scenarios. We also discuss the challenges and opportunities of conducting open and reproducible pandemic research. With over 10 million COVID-19 deaths reported worldwide, it's imperative that we continue developing and refining models to guide pandemic mitigation efforts and reduce future mortality rates. We invite the global scientific community to contribute to this critical endeavor and provide access to usable and easily modifiable code for the proposed model. This collaborative approach will help in accurately forecasting pandemic trends, guiding vaccination policies, and identifying effective intervention strategies to combat the ongoing pandemic. This research is an extension to our previous conference paper titled ``Mathematical Models for the SARS-CoV-2 Epidemic: An Analytical and Computational Overview'' presented at the MESA 2021 conference. We have made significant extensions to that work, including expanding the model to account for different vaccination roll-out scenarios, conducting a comprehensive analysis of global and national epidemiological data, and presenting multiple visualization tools. We have also made the code and data used in this research publicly available. This project is an expression of our commitment to open and accessible pandemic research. We believe that the ever-evolving nature of the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic requires an ongoing and collaborative response from the global scientific community, and we invite all interested researchers to contribute to this endeavor. We propose a new research direction for your consideration and look forward to your feedback, suggestions, and contributions. We are confident that a unified and collaborative effort will help in reducing mortality

Our new data hierarchy model, which we call Hierachy Storage System (HSS), is an advancement of existing DNA storage architectures. HSS divides data into three distinct levels, each utilizing a different type of base, making it an more efficient and adaptable technology. This innovative design enables targeted corrections and facilitates seamless maintenance of the base hierarchy without incurring the substantial costs of full-scale reencoding. Our research showcases a customized development of the CMSketch algorithm, a key HSS component, which significantly enhances the accuracy of base hierarchy assistance and yields a 90x% reduction in reencoding costs incurred during maintenance. When coupled with targeted correction strategies, this results in a 300-fold decrease in reencoding costs compared to conventional approaches. Our HSS architecture also supports efficient data hierarchies and facilitates fast reencoding, achieving a 3x speedup over existing solutions. These breakthroughs pave the way for a more versatile and adaptable DNA storage system. Our HSS system, rebranded as Adaptive Hierachy Storage (AHS), takes this a step further by introducing a dynamic data hierarchy that can be modified in response to changing access patterns, enabling optimal storage utilization and performance. Our AHS research yields a 4x and 10x improvement in read and write throughput respectively, and offers a highly adaptable and efficient solution for real-world applications. Our contributions are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/kuangqi/Adaptive-Hierarchy-Storage.

Acquiring high-quality images in mobile photography is made difficult by the conflicting demands of capturing both the brightest and darkest elements of a scene, which are typically separated by a certain logarithmic base.  Currently available mobile cameras process this problem using techniques that either divide the dynamic range of the image or capture it in multiple photographs.  However, neither of these methods is ideal as they either reduce the image's dynamic range or require the use of two cameras, one on each end of the mobile device, which are optically separated by 25 millimeters.  This expression presents a technique that overcomes these limitations by combining images captured with different exposure levels on a single CMOS sensor via a mobile phone.  The technique takes into account the sensor's characteristics, the shooting conditions, and the auto-focus and image-processing systems.  It results in a fusion technique that can capture a wide dynamic range, is compatible with 12 megapixel cameras, and can be implemented with a relatively small amount of hardware modifications.  It has been tested and showed its effectiveness with both natural and synthetic data.  The resulting system can capture a wide dynamic range, from 12 to 16 logarithmic base 10 units. The simplicial bundle construction resulting from an ordinary bundle equipped with simplicial structures can be interpreted through the perspective of the simplicial nerve. Specifically, given a bundle $E$ over a base space $B$ together with simplicial structures, we define a map $\phi$ that takes simplicial $n$-simplices in $B$ to bundles over $n$-simplices in $E$. This map has the property of preserving natural transformations. When the bundle $E$ is equipped with a group action, this map takes simplicial $n$-simplices in $B$ to the inner automorphisms of $E$ defined by $n$-simplices. Notably, when the bundle $E$ is topological and equipped with a group action, this map arises from the gequivariant universal bundle over the inner automorphism group of $E$. Specifically for the example of $E = \text{Diff}(M)$, the space of diffeomorphisms of a manifold $M$, we find that the cross-sectional bundle admits a natural group action equivalent to the action of $\text{SDiff}(M)$, the group of volume preserving diffeomorphisms of $M$. This reveals that $\text{SDiff}(M)$ is topologically equivalent to the inner automorphism group of $\text{Diff}(M)$. Additionally, we discover that this inner automorphism group contains the Hamiltonian diffeomorphisms of integral $2$-forms on $M$ as a subgroup. Lastly, we provide a characterization of the inner automorphism group arising from a particular Hamiltonian diffeomorphism, specifically showing it is topologically trivial for a hyperbolic surface $M$. This allows us to conclude that the volume preserving area diffeomorphisms of a hyperbolic surface are topologically simple, unlike their Euclidean counterparts. This study seeks to enhance the quality of erroneous positive data in visual relationship detection tasks. It has been observed that state-of-the-art models frequently misclassify unrelated object pairs as having a specific relationship. To achieve higher accuracy, it is necessary to improve the performance on challenging, low-frequency erroneous positive data. We propose a novel approach, dubbed the "Adversarial Model with Balanced Positive Sampling" (AMBPS), aimed at counteracting the bias favoring frequent positive data and manipulating the model to focus on less common erroneous pairs. In response to the proposed adversarial training method, the model learns to distinguish between correct and incorrect pairs. Furthermore, we introduce an anisotropy balanced positive sampling strategy to address the uneven distribution of positive data. This strategy prioritizes the selection of rare and difficult-to-classify positive data pairs. Our proposed method is tested on popular visual relationship detection datasets, including Visual Genome. The results show that AMBPS outperforms the current state-of-the-art models in terms of F-score, capturing the complex and dynamic structure of visual relationships. We're investigating the assembly of quiescent galaxies with lopsided stellar disks in a galaxy cluster that existed around 2.5 billion years after the Big Bang. By analyzing the mass distribution of 50 quiescent galaxies in a particular galaxy cluster at this stage of the universe's evolution, we've identified a significant group of galaxies with highly asymmetric stellar distributions and compact, spherical bulge formations. Notably, these galaxies with asymmetric stellar distributions also exhibit strong stellar bars and ring structures, indicating their disks aren't entirely lopsided. We propose a model where these disks developed a bar and ring structure, and then a prolate tidal torque caused their bulges to form more rapidly than their surrounding disks, given enough time. This theory is supported by observations of galaxies with asymmetric stellar distributions outside this particular cluster, and it offers valuable insights into the interplay between external gravitational influences, bar formation, and the development of bulges and rings in the centers of galaxies. Furthermore, it highlights the critical role of tidal interactions in shaping galaxies and their subsequent transformation into massive, bulge-dominated galaxies that are no longer actively creating new stars. These findings are consistent with some current studies suggesting that the primary driver of star formation cessation and the development of massive bulges and rones in the centers of galaxies isn't massive gas accretion, but rather the disruption of their disks through external gravitational influences, and the subsequent bar and ring formation it triggers. If this is the case, then it would challenge some of the current leading theories on the formation and evolution of galaxies, and it highlights the significance of continued observations and analyses, particularly with the upcoming Generation VI telescopes that will provide better resolution and allow for a more in-depth examination of these galaxies, and offer a clearer understanding of the universal principles governing their evolution.

Recently published research indicates that complex events such as solar flares may not be isolated occurrences but rather part of a broader pattern of repeated events that share a common underlying cause. Empirical studies support this notion, yet the events themselves are not well characterized due to limited data. This study aims to advance our understanding by analyzing decommissioned solar proton detectors' recordings from 1996 to 2005, revealing that large solar flares frequently recur within each other's 3 day intervals. Further analysis reveals that these events conform to a power law distribution, defying their expected exponential decline. If we assume its shape is that of a prolate spheroid, Acmonia's rotation speed would need an extraordinary boost of at least 30 times the typical angular momentum required for its current oval shape, suggesting it underwent a significant event. We explored possible causes for this momentum, considering factors like its formation, orbital history, and the effects of the Sun, Moon, and yors, but found them all insufficient to explain it. Even a massive impact that caused ingested material to spin fast enough for redistribution through gravitational forces would likely result in a different, more elongated shape. Therefore, we believe Acmonia's high spin likely results from a massive encounter with a similar-sized object, such as a collision with a asteroid of similar size, by inference, as we were unable to determine the angle of this encounter. This theory is supported by the uneven distribution of light from Acmonia during one rotation period, indicating an irregular shape that could only be explained by this kind of massive encounter. This conclusion is also consistent with similar observations of the spinning asteroids (1620) Geographos and (29075) 1950 DA. The possible encounter that led to this spin likely occurred when Acmonia was closer to the Sun than Mars, and could have happened within the past few million years, based on models of its orbital history. This kind of massive encounter would also result in the formation of a small moon, similar to how this happened with the Earth and the Moon, and could happen to other asteroids and planets, with resulting spin, irregular shapes, and small moons, as has been observed with the Pluto system and the asteroid Geographos. This study focuses on detecting false news, especially those that emerge suddenly, which is a critical issue in maintaining social platform trust. False information can spread rapidly and is difficult to remove once it gains traction. Existing approaches often prioritize accuracy over efficiency and struggle with evolving events. In contrast, we are addressing the efficient identification of newly emerging false news, rather than fact-checking each piece of news individually. Our goal is to develop a highly efficient model that can effectively identify new types of false news. To achieve this, we divide the model into two components: the first part learns general features from historical data, while the second part, which is responsible for false news detection, learns limited information from a small sample of recent data. Our novel Meta Neural Process Networks (Meta NPNs) allows the model to determine how to combine the two components based on the similarity between the test data and the recent false news examples. We conduct extensive experiments on three datasets and compare our model to multiple baselines, demonstrating the superior performance of our model. The code is available online at https://github.com/ghrua/Meta-NPN. The model's efficiency in identifying emerging false news makes it suitable for dynamic environments where new false information emerges constantly. This model's ability to adapt to new data quickly also enables it to excel in other domain-specific tasks such as detecting newly emerging spam emails. The model's performance can be improved by incorporating more effective optimization algorithms and using more sophisticated hyperparameter settings, as demonstrated in the appendix. A higher-order signal processing technique known as multirate filter banks has numerous applications in various communication systems, offering advantages such as robustness against carrier frequency offset and pulse collisions in multiple-access interference. However, the availability of Golay complementary pairs is limited to a small set of sequences, significantly limiting their practical use. This paper breaks new ground in the field of filter banks by introducing the concept of polyphase Golay complementary sets, and we successfully create large-sized pairs of Golay sequences using a technique called polyphase sequence partitioning. This innovation enables us to generate a vast array of complementary pairs and even matrices of Golay sequences, surpassing the constraints of traditional methods. We also generate and list a significant number of new sequence pairs in a compact and easily accessible format for future use. This work paves the way for an exciting area of research and we invite and encourage our peers to collaborate and contribute to this field. This paper is an expanded version of a presentation that appeared in the proceedings of the IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Signal and Image Processing, Alexandria, Egypt in 2021. We have updated it to include additional sequence pairs and new types of complementary sets. This work is also associated with a companion website that provides further information and resources. Complex systems, encompassing social networks, the human brain, and transportation systems, among others, are characterized by intricate interactions between their components. Because of their composite nature, these interactions aren't fixed but vary significantly over time. This paper points out that in contrast to traditional dynamical systems, where connections between components and their state evolution are constant and well defined, complex systems are better represented using graph neural networks to capture the dynamic and changing relationships and how they affect the components' state evolution. We present a non linear state update network, capable of generating a series of interactions represented as directed edges between components, as well as a set of state update rules represented as directed edges with weights that represent the state transformation functions. We also introduce a framework to build a unified system model. This involves first training a set of state update networks based on historical data of the components' state evolution, then training a graph neural network on the temporal interactions between components. This network generates a weighted and directed graph that represents the dynamic connections and their impact on the state transformation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by applying it to a real life problem, specifically a traffic dynamics problem. This involves training a set of state update networks and a graph neural network on historical data of the components' state evolution and the interactions between them. GP 2 is a graph-based language designed for efficient program analysis and verification, leveraging graph transformation systems to their fullest potential. However, efficiently developing correct and verified programs using GP 2 can be challenging, primarily due to the complex nature of its type system and extensive need for explicit type annotations. To overcome these obstacles and make GP 2 more accessible, we developed an enhanced type checker, known as the "big" GP 2 type checker, which includes a type inference feature to streamline program development. This type checker is accompanied by a "small" type checker, retaining the original GP 2 syntax and semantics for verification purposes. Both type checkers are part of the GP 2 compiler suite, which also includes a runtime environment for executing GP 2 programs. This execution environment provides a simple and type-safe way to execute GP 2 transformations within a Java application. The GP 2 compiler and runtime are both freely available open-source tools. The development of the GP 2 compiler was funded by the DFG within the Artificial Intelligence Project ENTRiPerS. The researchers behind the GP 2 compiler recently presented their work at the International Symposium on Practical Aspects of Declarative Languages, co-located with the European Conference on Programming Languages and Systems. The GP 2 compiler is capable of compiling GP 2 programs into high-performance Java methods that can be utilized within a variety of analysis and verification tools. The development of the GP 2 compiler facilitates efficient program development, coupled with type safety and verification capabilities, as demonstrated through a technical case study involving the development of a scalable static program analysis tool. The GP 2 compiler provides an exemplary solution for other researchers and the scientific community to emulate in their own verification and analysis tools. A key aspect of these networks is their ability to establish a mapping between two different types of data, thanks to their parametrized and non-parametrized components. Previous studies have explored these networks in isolation, but there's been little work done on comparing and contrasting them. This study fills this gap by examining two identical neural networks in separate tasks and showing that by combining their parametrized components, we can compare and contrast the features extracted from each network. A numerical analysis confirms the validity of this approach and demonstrates its potential uses in feature comparison and selection. Moreover, this study introduces a novel method for selecting the appropriate structure for these networks, which in turn enables the comparison and contrast of different features. This comparison and contrast can occur using a variety of methods, including those that are non-parametric and learned from data. In a numerical analysis, this study shows that the features extracted from these networks, when combined, enable a better comparison and contrast of the data than other feature extraction methods. Working with nominal data poses a multiple-testing problem when performing statistical tests or selecting features. Many methods have been developed to handle this issue, but they typically require the number of categories per variable to be kept relatively small. The Group Lasso has been a popular and effective technique for reducing dimensions in the context of continuous features but hasn't been much use in dealing with nominal data. A way to combine the Group Lasso with a Firth's type of penalty has been explored and differs based on the maximum number of categories per variable, offering a flexible model known as EFEN. This model can accommodate a wide range of nominal data structures. A gap exists in available research as it hasn't been paired with a suitable estimation procedure. This study addresses this issue by developing an EM algorithm for estimating the Group Lasso Firth penalty. A simulation study demonstrates the efficacy of this approach. The method has been applied to real-world data from genetics. Code has been provided.

Recent large language models have demonstrated superior performance in various tasks, yet the underlying reasoning behind their successes remains poorly understood. We introduce a novel assessment framework called ABILITY, which evaluates the structural integration of background knowledge within LLMs by posing targeted tests that engage both their knowledge and reasoning capabilities. We selectively train a subset of LLM tasks that concentrate on their knowledge structure and reject those that are largely resolved through simple heuristics or straightforward computation. Each ability in ABILITY is composed of multiple specific tests designed to assess different knowledge dimensions, including but not limited to factual knowledge, categorization, relationships and patterns. We assemble a comprehensive set of 50 tasks that cover a broad spectrum of LLM knowledge dimensions and systematically assess four prominent LLM models across various abilities, revealing that their capabilities are highly diverse and influenced by parameters such as model size and training data. We also show that certain LLM abilities can be developed through tailored training on limited datasets. Notably, our research uncovers a striking contrast between T5-based models and tLM-based models, with the former exhibiting a more comprehensive knowledge base but difficulty in accessing it, and the latter showcasing a more efficient knowledge-accessing mechanism but a more limited knowledge base. Our findings and the ABILITY assessment platform are valuable resources for both the broader LLM research community and potential practitioners, offering insights to guide model selection, identifying areas for further development, and providing a structured framework for evaluating the knowledge dimensions of LLMs. We make the ABILITY platform publicly available at https://ability.is.gd/. High-resolution vector maps are gaining popularity, and their widespread adoption is necessitating efficient rendering techniques to maintain real-time performance. In this case, we're focusing on line junction anti-aliasing, a critical aspect for achieving a smooth and visually appealing map display. However, due to the complex nature of Bezier surfaces and their substantial computational requirements, developing an anti-aliasing solution has proven challenging. To overcome this limitation, we've introduced a novel algorithm that provides effective anti-aliasing for line junctions using simple and lightweight operations. By minimizing the number of pixels modified during rendering, our solution achieves significant performance improvements while delivering high-quality anti-aliasing results. To further enhance the map display experience, we've explored additional techniques for reducing the computational load during rendering. The resulting anti-aliasing and optimization approach has been demonstrated to offer substantial gains in both performance and visual quality for real-world vector maps. In particular, our solution has been shown to yield a 5-10x performance improvement and achieves a 30-60fps frame rate on a range of popular mapping applications. In addition to its applicability to mapping applications, the introduced anti-aliasing technique is equally relevant to other vector graphics contexts that demand high-performance rendering. In fact, our analysis has uncovered that this approach can be effectively applied to a broad category of Bezier surface anti-aliasing problems. In multi-channel speech processing, improving the quality of individual channels can significantly enhance overall performance.
A new Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) is proposed to address this challenge.
This model combines two Convolution Recurrent Networks, each processing a separate path of the short-time Fourier transform output.
Convolution Recurrent Networks are chosen for their ability to handle spectral distortions and over-lapping talkers.
The DPCRN model yields a weight that is used to control the blending of the input and the predicted signal.
Experiments on the 5.1 multi-channel DNS test condition show that DPCRN delivers 0.25 in speech intelligibility and 1.85 in mean opinion score improvement. Code for this work is available at github.com/kuangruwen/DPCRN.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A novel two-fluid model, which splits air into a separate fluid for convection, has demonstrated the ability to accurately replicate atmospheric convection while sidestepping the traditional issue of convective instability. The present research seeks to further develop this model by creating a simple single-column simulation capable of modeling non-buoyant aerosols. It successfully replicates both clean and aerosol-affected Rayleigh-Benard convection through the introduction of a sublayer model, allowing it to account for the thermal and mechanical effects of the aerosol particles. Ultimately, the model is compared to actual laboratory experiments of Rayleigh-Benard convection with aerosols, demonstrating a high level of accuracy in both clean and contaminated conditions. The resulting simulation code is user-friendly and can be easily integrated into existing weather and climate simulation frameworks, providing a substantial advancement towards the development of multi-fluid models of atmospheric convection. We investigate three Jaynes-Cummings systems that each contain one of three non-entangled qubits. By analyzing the collective dynamics of these systems, we identify a specific authenticating process that generates genuine tripartite entanglement from the initial state of the qubits. This process is made up of two distinct phases: during the initial phase, a highly discordant state is created, while in the second phase, a genuinely tripartite entangled state is generated. This state can be manipulated through a variety of means, including the use of a specific type of laser known as a squeezer. This research provides multiple innovative solutions for generating not only bipartite but also tripartite entangled states, offering valuable insights that can be applied to a wide range of scenarios involving authenticating and generating entanglement. This study is also conducted in a way that allows it to be easily extended to the study of multiple Jaynes-Cummings systems that each contain two non-entangled qubits. Recently, a new field called "in-air" video forecasting has gained significant attention and can be applied in 360-degree virtual tourism. In this context, users can move their head within a video to obtain more historical data, making traditional methods less effective. Our novel approach, caption-based viewport forecasting, utilizes text descriptions accompanying the video to capture users' previous viewing areas and forecast their future head positions. Unlike many current approaches, our method disregards the "in-air" history and utilizes a multi-task learning model that combines caption-guided and autoencoder-based predictions to forecast future head positions. Our experiment showed that, by excluding "in-air" history, our approach achieved comparable results to models using that information. Moreover, our method can be applied in a more scalable way with limited training data, outperforming the current state-of-the-art in various evaluation metrics. As a pioneering work in this field, our approach has vast potential applications, particularly in 360-degree virtual tourism. As such, we also explored an instance called caption-based streaming forecast, which is more suitable for low-bandwidth streaming environments, and demonstrated its effectiveness. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/ghrjy/CaptionForecasting.

Reusing previously developed machine learning models in a black-box setting can significantly streamline the development of new models. This research focuses on taking advantage of this beneficial approach by introducing a method called Knowledge Transfer via Optimization (KTO). Within the KTO framework, it is assumed that a model's behavior can be represented by a decision-making process, though the specifics of this process are unknown. By considering multiple possible models, the knowledge transferred is viewed as a subset of all possible decision-making processes. As a result, the KTO framework is capable of adapting to unknown model characteristics and deciding on the most suitable models for a particular problem. To effectively use the KTO framework, it is recommended to train a set of diverse models that can serve as a basis for decision-making in a black-box setting. To illustrate the effectiveness of the KTO framework, it was applied to designing acoustic models for speech synthesis, where it demonstrated superior performance over alternative methods. Additionally, the framework showed potential in other decision-making domains such as audio classification and natural language generation. It is worth noting that the KTO framework can be implemented using just the output of the model, without access to its internal workings, making it a convenient and versatile tool. The resulting models produced in this research were found to be not only superior to alternative methods but also on par with state-of-the-art models, including transformer-based acoustic models. The code for the KTO framework along with example experiments is available online. The diversity of models that can be combined within the KTO framework has significant implications, given that there is currently a lack of standardized model architectures across different research areas. It is also possible to use the KTO framework for zero-shot learning, though this would require models that possess this capability by nature. The paper discusses three such models, each with its own distinct characteristics, and demonstrates their effectiveness in various tasks. It is worth noting that the term zero-shot learning is used here in a more general sense than its traditional definition, which typically implies the presence of class names during training. The code for the zero-shot learning models along with the KTO framework is available online. The results presented in this paper have not been submitted or published elsewhere. The KTO framework has numerous potential applications and extensions, such as using pre-trained language models, generating multiple models using different optimization techniques, and exploring its connection to meta-learning. Constructing the lattice of submodules of a module that has no repeated composition factors is relatively straightforward as it is generated by inclusion relations between modules with defined and distinct composition factors. However, determining the lattice of submodules for a module that has repeated composition factors, such as $M^n$, where $n > 1$, is more complicated and needs a different approach. Our work presents an algorithm for reconstructing the lattice of submodules of a module that has no repeated composition factors at its peak, using a set of covering modules as input. These covering modules are defined as modules with exactly one composition factor that covers the peak module in question. Alternatively, if all the covering modules are known, there is a method for directly constructing the lattice of submodules. We apply and extend the concept of $e$-extremal modules to enable a second approach for constructing the lattice of submodules for a module with distinct composition factors at its peak, being formed by a set of modules with specific and defined composition factors. This second method allows us to derive the lattice of submodules for modules such as $S(n,\lambda)$, where $n$ is the multiplicity of the highest weight weight $\lambda$. We demonstrate and illustrate our method with an example, specifically the module $M^{(3,2)}$. Our algorithm is versatile and can be implemented on a computer, providing a tangible tool for constructing the lattice of submodules for any module with no repeated composition factors at its peak. This is demonstrated with an analysis of the lattice of submodules for the module $M^{(3,2)}$, derived using both methods and Quiver -- a software tool designed for this purpose -- showing that our method yields results that are consistent with the output from Quiver. We conclude by discussing potential future developments and generalizations of our method. This work is dedicated to the memory of our friend and colleague, Stephen Parker. MongoDB is a widely used, document-oriented NoSQL database that has gained considerable popularity in recent years. As a result of its rising usage, ensuring the consistency of MongoDB data has become increasingly vital. One approach to achieving this consistency is through transactional integrity, ensured by validating transactions according to a set of predicates defined by the user. Despite its benefits, implementing consistency in MongoDB proves challenging, especially considering its non-blocking nature, vast scalability, and capability to handle high throughput. In our research, we investigated the opportunities for extending MongoDB's snapshot isolation layer to enforce these predicates and validated our approach by conducting rigorous testing. These tests comprised modifying MongoDB's snapshot isolation layer, developing a set of sample applications to demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of our approach, as well as validating the accuracy of our predicate validation stack by running a throughput-oriented benchmark on it. In addition, we explored and refined our approach by identifying areas where further optimization is possible, and we discussed the limitations of our research, along with potential paths for modifying MongoDB's commit layer. In a real-world scenario, we demonstrated the capability of our approach to ensure the transactional integrity of a MongoDB database used in conjunction with Apache Airflow, and made available the code for our predicate validation stack on GitHub. In the process, we compared our approach with other consistency maintenance techniques, including those that rely on application-level adherence to consistency rules, and discussed the various definitions and implementations of snapshot isolation. In a real-world application, we set up a test environment where MongoDB is used in conjunction with Apache Airflow, and validated our approach by conducting thorough testing of this setup. In our research, we validated the accuracy and efficiency of our predicate validation stack, and made available the code for this stack, along with the test data used in our testing, on GitHub. In the process, we discussed the opportunities and challenges associated with extending the snapshot isolation layer of NoSQL databases, and the various definitions and implementations of snapshot isolation. We develop a method for converting spectral data into potential data within the framework of monodromy-free Schrödinger operators. This conversion approach enables us to determine both complex-valued potential functions U(λ) in the complex plane and real-valued potential functions v(x) in the real line, given their respective spectral data. The complex-valued potential functions U(λ) are constructed using generalized Hermite polynomials, providing an analytical extension for the standard Titchmarsh koerbe formula. Furthermore, real-valued potential functions v(x) are derived from the complex-valued counterparts via the use of Cayley-Hamilton theorem applications. These constructions serve as fundamental building blocks for analyzing the monodromy-free Schrödinger problem in both the complex and real domains. A curious crinkling noise emitted by an adhesive tape as it's unwound has been investigated to uncover its underlying structural patterns. Utilizing both human ears to detect patterns and a motion sensor to analyze the vibrations, we found that the sound's intensity follows a random, Poisson-like distribution during the initial unwinding phase, but suddenly shifts to a highly organized, periodic pattern as the winding becomes more loose. This transition to a more complex, non-random state defies conventional explanations and highlights the hidden potential for order in seemingly chaotic, disordered systems. Synchronizing the sensor data with video footage provides a three-dimensional visualization that confirms the emergence of a periodic, helical structure within the tape roll. This surprising discovery opens the door for exploring the intricate relationships between randomness and order in diverse, naturally occurring systems. A simple model is also proposed to illustrate the origin of this periodic order. The unique acoustic characteristics of the unwinding process may serve as a natural demonstration for physics-related education. The underlying principles and their broader implications are discussed in the paper's concluding section. The research behind this paper was conducted in 2019 at the University of Tokyo. The authors propose the name "Tape Tonometer" for a device that measures sound-generated pressure, which may have further applications in music-related fields. The paper's appendices provide additional information on the model's analysis, suggestions for classroom activities, and a related anecdotal experience.
