Our analysis reveals that certain materials can exhibit a rare and exotic property - a type of energy band that touches only once, yet at a "squared" point of intersection. This unique feature, which occurs in 3D space and is different from the "T" or "X" shapes commonly associated with Weyl semimetals, is however prone to failure under external stress, losing its exceptional properties. To mitigate this drawback, we propose an innovative idea to deliberately introduce small distortions in the energy band structure, effectively elevating its point of contact to a tiny "loop" of intersection. This localized modification has significant consequences, creating multiple minimal points of contact, isolated from one another, and thus dubbed the "square-root" Weyl semimetal phenomenon. This novel state can be stabilized in various low-stress scenarios, enabled by an array of stress-inducible materials with both all-around and anisotropic responses. This breakthrough discovery and its versatile realization in various forms offer new avenues for scientific investigation and potential applications. This research represents a collaborative effort between theoretical physicists and experimental engineers who designed and conducted trials on model materials, providing a comprehensive understanding and actionable blueprints for further development. This finding and its associated physics can be applied to a wide range of materials, including transition metal dichalcogenides, silicene, germanene, phosphorene, and few-layer black phosphorus. This novel square-root Weyl semimetal phenomenon and its associated energy band structures may also be realized in other areas of condensed matter and particle physics, offering a rich area for continued exploration. This research was conducted by a large team of authors from multiple institutions around the world. The intense internal structure of ultra-high power laser pulses hinders their effectiveness for medical treatments involving specific tissue types. A magnetized plasma can filter out the unwanted parts of a laser pulse by separating its different polarization components based on their individual speeds within the plasma. However, previously studied configurations have limited ability to enhance the desired component's intensity due to the limited extent of plasma required. We introduce a new, concurrence-based model where two counter-propagating laser pulses with cross-polarization properties are used, allowing the desired component to be both filtered and intensified as they interact within the same plasma area. Our simulations show that at appropriate intensities, the 10% most powerful linearly polarized pulses can be both purified (mainly in the p-polarization component) and amplified (up to 2 times) within the same range of parameters. This new concept has the potential to significantly improve the therapeutic applications of ultra-intense laser systems. Additionally, this idea can be applied to other problems that involve intense laser pulses and could broaden the capabilities of plasma-based concurrence effects. A proposed experimental setup is also presented.

The third generation of gravitational wave detectors will significantly enhance the capabilities of gravitational wave observatories by emitting signals with greater precision, a broader frequency range, and a much longer duration. To take full advantage of these improvements, machine learning models that identify signals from neutron star-neutron star, black hole-neutron star, and black hole-black hole mergers need to be highly accurate and capable of distinguishing between these mergers. We developed a set of six separate neural network detectors that can recognize and categorize signals from these mergers with high accuracy, far exceeding the capabilities of the current LIGO/Virgo detectors. We demonstrated how these neural networks can be trained on a limited number of signals with a low signal-to-Noise Ratio and be highly effective at identifying and labeling all mergers with greater energy in the $13-200$ Hz frequency range. We also showed that these models can be trained to prioritize the identification of specific types of mergers over others, and that they excel at predicting the masses of the merging objects with a level of precision that is commensurate with the accuracy of the detectors used to measure these masses. For robots to effectively navigate complex environments, multiple layers of information from the same sensor can be utilized in a combined method of navigation known as "multi-layer navigation". This approach combines the results of different path planning algorithms using weighted averages, which simplifies the robot's control system but introduces challenges in determining optimal weights. A common issue with the current methods of determining these weights is that they typically consider the performance of the navigation system on a macro level, over extended periods of time, which makes them unsuitable for tasks that require immediate decision making, such as obstacle avoidance. Our solution presents a technique called "sonar blending" that provides a real-time weighted average of sonar sensor readings with a direct application in navigation, demonstrating a notable improvement in the robot's ability to navigate through tight spaces. We further combine this technique with a custom priority layer navigation system, demonstrating a notable increase in the robot's ability to successfully navigate through confined spaces on its own. Traditionally, annotated datasets serve as gold standards for emerging technologies, but their stability is rarely considered due to their cost of creation. In fact, annotated datasets can inevitably progress as linguistic knowledge evolves. This research focuses on emotion-related annotated data and employs a BERT-based approach to guide revisers in refining existing annotations by leveraging three levels of revision guidance. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, we developed a tool that enables mass revision efforts. Utilizing this tool, we collected a large-scale, revised dataset spanning 10,000 sentences. Furthermore, we found that the simplicity of our approach allows it to be applied to various annotation tasks. To further establish the value of our approach, we compared it to a baseline method employing a single, randomly selected annotator. The results of this comparison showed that our approach yields more precise revisions. To expand on these findings, we explored the relationship between our revision scores and various linguistic metrics. To showcase the versatility of our approach, we demonstrated its applicability to different annotation tasks, including those involving a BERT-based evaluation system. This research is characterized by its interdisciplinary nature, falling within the fields of human-computer interaction, emotions and cognition, and natural language processing. In conclusion, our BERT-supported annotation revision framework offers a versatile tool capable of guiding the revision of annotated data, primarily emotion-related data, which can be employed in various contexts, both within and beyond this specific domain. This framework, coupled with the revised dataset of 10,000 sentences, has been made available to the public. This research paves the way for further developments, such as the creation of more stable, less prone to bias annotated data, which can be achieved by implementing a continuous revision process. This process can be facilitated by establishing clear guidelines for revisers and developing a system for tracking and managing the evolution of annotated data. Ultimately, this research has implications for various real-world applications, including but not limited to chatbots, sentiment analysis, and emotional cognition studies. This research develops an integrated framework that combines finite mixture models, geometric probability, and Choquet theory. We begin by reviewing the basic concepts of mixture models and identify their connection to support functions and subdifferentials. We then apply these concepts to analyze and solve common optimization problems related to mixture models. Next, we examine geometric probability, starting with the definition of mixed volumes and their relationship to the Minkowski mixed volume. We then delve into the generalization of mixed volumes in projective geometry and the associated valuation. We explore the connection between projective geometry and mixture models, specifically generalised mixture volumes and their connection to the Łojasiewicz exponent of a polynomial. We also discuss how this integrated framework can be applied to study the behaviour of random variables and polynomials. Finally, we outline the potential future developments in this integrated framework. This work is the result of discussions and collaborations with several researchers, particularly Philippe G. By analyzing $TESS$ data, the team established that the star rotates in about 12.48 days and has an obliquity of $45.70^{\circ}$. A type of surface roughness called intrinsic texture occurs frequently in nature and is present on surfaces, including those of lotus leaves and sandstones. Intrinsic texture can influence the coefficient of friction when a solid slides over another solid with the same surface texture. However, the impact of intrinsic texture on the movement of a solid over a soft and deformable surface, which changes in response to pressure and tension, is not well understood. In our study, we used a glass slide with a consistent intrinsic texture to observe how it affects the movement of a soap film. We found that the texture on the glass slide is capable of creating localized areas of stickiness or stiffness at the interface with the soap film, which in turn affects the sliding behavior. This interaction allows for three different modes of movement: the generation of lines or the creation of bubbles through a process known as blister growth, and a third mode called granular, which is characterized by the movement of the interface in a rough and uneven manner. This last mode of movement, granular, can occur at both low and high speeds of sliding. This interplay between the texture and the moving interface also raises fundamental questions about the appropriate way to define and calculate the coefficient of friction. This issue holds significance not just for the interaction between the glass slide and the soap film but also for similar interactions with other soft and deformable surfaces, including skin and other biological tissues. This research adds a new perspective to the understanding of texture-induced friction that goes beyond its influence on the mechanical properties of the surfaces involved. We have recently proposed a novel CNN architecture known as PSO-ASC, which has efficiently been applied in both image classification and detection tasks. Building upon this architecture, we introduced a new model named AD-ASC, which adds an auxiliary branch to extract heatmaps and incorporates an outlier detection module using maximum likelihood estimation to identify samples with abnormal class probabilities. We further developed an algorithm called AD-ASC-S, which utilizes the Salient Response Theory to update the heatmaps and refine the outlier detection results. We then explored a combination of the AD-ASC-S and PSO-ASC models known as AD-ASC-S/PSO, which outperformed the existing state-of-the-art methods in both image classification and detection tasks. We also demonstrated the versatility of this model by applying it to a real-world problem, namely identifying malignant skin carcinoma samples from a large dataset. The resulting model achieved remarkable performance, yielding a 10-fold improvement in accuracy compared to the conventional CNN methods. We open-sourced the AD-ASC-S/PSO architecture on GitHub, which is also suitable for other outlier detection tasks. In neural machine translation, the attention model is typically designed to focus on source language information to enhance target language production. We challenge this conventional approach by exploring the benefits of a look-forward attention model that focuses on target language information to improve source language understanding and subsequent production. We incorporate the reverse attention model in two ways and evaluate its impact on baselines, including transformer and convolutional encoder-decoder models. Our results show that a simple look-forward attention mechanism integrated into the decoder's attention weighting can be beneficial, but its effectiveness depends on the specific task. To enhance stability and performance, we propose an augmented model that incorporates the reverse attention weights into the decoder's feedforward network, achieving the best results among all methods tested. Our analysis indicates that the look-forward attention mechanism facilitates the generation of diverse phrases, as confirmed by an evaluation using the similarity metric between generated sequences and reference translations. We also analyze the search patterns of look-forward attention and demonstrate that its mechanism complements conventional left-to-right decoding patterns. Ultimately, our proposed augmented model delivers superior performance over baseline encoders and decoders in machine translation tasks. Our code is available online at GitHub.

This work develops novel methods for conducting multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis on data from different dimensional domains. We employ ridged representations to extend the technique for analyzing data from a single domain to a comparison of multiple domains, and then use these representations to identify common dynamics across all domains. We further explore the application of these representations in determining the distinct dynamics of each individual domain. Our research utilizes both artificial and real-world data, including a case study on the North Atlantic Oscillation across multiple latitude bands. We find that the distinct domain-specific dynamics capture unique features of each domain without being overlapping with the common dynamics, and our results are validated by other techniques. Our approach provides tools for researchers to explore and compare the singular spectrum across different dimensional domains, and our code is available on github.com/singularitylab/mfsse.

GCNNs, which effectively capture local structural information in graphs, have seen vast practical applications. However, the intricate math behind their convolution operation has hindered our understanding of the underlying reasoning for their ability to capture node-level features. To address this knowledge gap, we propose a novel GCNN architecture, "Match-Conv", that incorporates a filtering approach in both spatial and spectral graph convolution layers to provide a side-view of the underlying operations. By ascribing distinct roles to learning and representation, Match-Conv enables an explicit analysis of how features are captured and allows for the selection of optimal convolution methods based on the underlying graph characteristics. Leveraging the insights gained from our model, we conduct an in-depth examination of the spectral convolution operation, demonstrating the equivalence of the standard implementation to a first-order Tikhonov regularization. Additionally, we introduce a novel Spectral Convolution called "Damped one-order Tikhonov regularization", examine its uniqueness characteristics, and demonstrate the superiority of Match-Conv in several benchmark tasks. With Match-Conv, we aim to contribute a replicable and comprehensible methodology for understanding and analyzing the underlying principles and operations of GCNNs. All the code for Match-Conv is available at https://github.com/ghrua/Match-Conv.

Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive identification of tissue pathologies by analyzing the mechanical characteristics of tissues. Despite its advantages, accurate displacement measurement remains a challenge, primarily due to the limited aperture size in many ultrasound elastography systems and the resulting poor lateral resolution. This issue can be addressed through a novel Virtual Origin Synthetic Aperture (VOSA) method, which employs two short-duration sweeps to achieve precise and rapid displacement estimation across the aperture. By applying a time-reversal acoustic focusing technique, the sweep signals are re-radiated from the aperture, resulting in a synthetic aperture that significantly exceeds the physical one. This approach is demonstrated using a phantom and a real-time elastography system, yielding high-resolution images and accurate estimation of lateral displacement. The results show that the proposed VOSA method offers superior resolution and matches the performance of the conventional system in controlled conditions. This technique has the potential to be adapted for a range of elastography systems, enabling a substantial improvement in the lateral resolution of elastography images. This research also presents a numerical model of the VOSA method, which can be utilized for initial system protocol validation before conducting the actual experiments. This model facilitates the assessment and optimization of the sweep duration, focal zone, and aperture size, among other variables, through the analysis of discrete sweep data. This validation is critical, given the complex interaction between the sweep duration, the system's frequency response, and the resulting displacement estimation, among other factors. This study further explores and presents a novel approach to estimating the origin location from the reconstructed pressure fields, which is a key aspect of the VOSA method. This estimation is necessary because the accurate placement of the virtual origin is crucial for obtaining high-resolution images and is influenced by the reflectivity distribution within the scanned object. This distribution can vary significantly across different objects and tissues, complicating the problem further. This challenge is addressed through the development of a robust and automated algorithm that can handle a wide range of objects and scenarios, based on a combination of the principles of time-reversal acoustic focusing and the distribution of reflected ultrasound signals. This algorithm enables the estimation of the origin location from the reconstructed pressure fields, as well as the validation of the proposed VOSA method against conventional synthetic aperture systems, through a numerical analysis of the reflectivity distribution, sweep data, and resulting displacement estimation. Humans and computers collaborate through algorithms, yet our language systems seem to prioritize expressing to humans over instructing computers. To address this issue, we propose a new hypothesis – that people follow algorithms based on a set of rational rules and simple common sense – and support it with a comprehensive analysis. To express these guidelines, we developed a one-step translation process that converts existing algorithm descriptions into a new, intuitive format called Pseudocode of Proportional Intention. In a controlled study, participants who used this format demonstrated significant improvements in accurately completing tasks. Our findings also offer practical suggestions for creating more effective algorithm instructions. To facilitate further research and real-world applications, we are making Pseudocode of Proportional Intention available to the public. In the context of a dynamic $k$-means clustering among changing datasets, we've developed an efficient algorithm that balances data points into nearly perfectly sized groups and minimizes the total distance between points and their assigned cluster centers. This efficient algorithm has two main characteristics: it can process new data arrivals in roughly linear time and guarantees an optimal solution for a smaller, more manageable subproblem. We've proven that this algorithm's groups are within a small factor of the optimal groups, specifically a factor of $O(\sqrt{k}\log k)$, which is demonstrated through a hypothetical optimal group structure known as a centered ball partition. We've also shown that in a decreasing dataset scenario, we can reduce the factor to $O(k)$ by creating a new data arrival order that prioritizes points further from the existing centers. Additionally, we've established a lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{k})$ on the factor of any dynamic algorithm for a specific centered ball partition, thereby establishing the correctness of our factor guarantee for a particular scenario as a upper against a relevant lower. We've implemented this algorithm as a part of a larger dynamic $k$-means algorithm and compared it to several alternative approaches through a clustering-based text classification experiment using twenty datasets. We've also applied this algorithm to a real-life customer segmentation analysis task. All implementation code is publicly available. This research addresses an important challenge in developing precise particle colliders, specifically those using high-energy muons, where accurately measuring the properties of subatomic particles, particularly vectors, becomes increasingly difficult due to limited acceptance in detectors, final states that are complex, and competing background processes. To tackle this problem, our innovative approach leverages machine learning on fast generator-level simulations of collisions to predict the properties of particles, achieved through a novel "level 0" estimation process called Vector Boson Estimation, or VBE. By utilizing VBE, we can significantly reduce the number of actual collisions that need to be physically analyzed by detectors from an estimated 10^9 to 10^7, thus enabling the development of more effective collision energies and facilitating discoveries with smaller detectors. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that efficient estimation can be flexible and tailored to specific particles, facilitating the development of universal and bespoke VBE tools. This breakthrough has significant implications for future colliders using high-energy muons, such as the Future Circular Collider, Muon Collider Options, and the Muon Accelerator Program, among others. Our code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/VectorBosonEstimation/.

Our empirical evaluations on a wide range of games support these findings and show that a modular system often yields a 50% improvement in performance compared to a non-modular system. We also observe that a modular system allows it to easily accommodate a wide range of tasks, from 3 to 60, in games such as Atari. Recently generated technologies such as speech enhancement, music source separation, and audio duet restoration can produce a separate posterior output while producing an input. This output can be used as a more precise mask to remove background noise and unwanted components from an original signal. Inverse technologies like these are different from traditional signal processing enhancements like noise reduction algorithms. In this research, a novel method called the Posterior Producer Network (PPN) is introduced. PPN produces a high-quality posterior output in just one pass through the model. This model consists of multiple conditional GANs that work together to correct overfitting and generate more precise results. Experimental evaluations using separate posterior outputs and masks showed that PPN outperforms existing state-of-the-art models including multi-pass conditional GANs and commercial industry solutions. Code for the PPN model is available on GitHub at https://github.com/openaustralia/PPN. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch-related issues and extensive training data requirements. To overcome these limitations, QPNet introduces a pitch-sensitive dilated convolution layer with a two-component structure, combining a pitch-independent part and a pitch-dependent part using a learned weight. The results show that QPNet excels in both small and large-scale text-to-speech synthesis settings, offering a lightweight and efficient alternative for various speech generation tasks. The bicategorical shadow conjecture is a highly regarded proposal that aims to expand the shadows concept initially introduced by Kazhdan-Lusztig and later developed by Soergel within the context of Coxeter systems and certain subspaces of the bar complex. By taking a step back from this context, our research provides a more fundamental interpretation of the shadows. We demonstrate that they are directly related to certain combinatorial elements called polyhedra, and show how these polyhedra can be matched with the polynomials they represent through a bicategorical construction. This construction can be seen as a projection that loses memory of the roots, yet surprisingly retains the information needed for calculating the coefficients of the Eulerian operator. This in turn leads to an accessible proof of the Kazhdan-Lusztig polynomial positivity conjecture, which has been a longstanding challenge. This approach also introduces a new fundamental operation called the bicategorical track, and shows how it can be used to extend and refine the shadows beyond their original context. This extension and refinement is so powerful that it can be used to prove and generalize the positivity conjecture, which now applies to a much broader category of polynomials. This includes but is not limited to, the Khovanov-Rozansky link homology, torus knot and cable link invariants, as well as the rational Hagihara, Deodhar, and extended Deodhar inequalities, all of which are related to the same underlying principle using different variables. This research and all its results were initially obtained in the thesis submitted by the author to the University of California, Santa Cruz in 2019. This work has been reviewed and updated since then, and all the results have been confirmed as holding true. This approach simplifies the covariant field equations derived from variational principles, offering a linear connection between the harmonic tensor and the symmetric tensor in the gravity sector while maintaining full covariance. A brief review of harmonic gauge theory is provided, followed by an in-depth examination of its applications in massive gravity, symmetric gravity, and $f(R)$-gravity. These examples demonstrate how the harmonic gauge theory can be utilized to handle these theories with massive degrees of freedom. Moreover, we discuss the (harmonic) non-linear gauge theory as a means of comparing with earlier works and provide an introductory overview of this framework's key features. This paper is intended to serve as a concise, self-contained account of the harmonic gauge(s) in harmonic gauge theory, suitable for inclusion in the proceedings of the "Gravity, Astrophysics and Cosmology from High to Low Resolution" conference held in Bologna, Italy, 2019. Despite its standalone purpose, it is also designed to be a companion to the lecture notes presented to the conference attendees. These notes and the accompanying paper share a harmonious relationship, with the notes focusing on the fundamental principles of harmonic gauge theory and the paper centered on its applications in substantial gravity.

This equivalence holds under two circumstances: firstly, when the moduli spaces share an isomorphism after removing their irreducible components of lowest dimensions; or secondly, in a scenario where one space contains the other, each with an added set of coordinates, within a particular dimensional framework. As a direct application of this principle, we prove that certain singularities, those defined by non-degenerate arrangements of lines in a plane with specific intersection properties, possess unique invariant properties that distinguish them from one another.
